```text
Excellent. Let me now compile my findings in a concise report under 400 words.

## Survey Report: TC358743 HDMI-to-CSI-2 Bridge Driver for MPLAB Harmony SAM9X75

### **1) Marvin Project** (`/Users/gregmrozek/Projects/microchip/guitar-pic/firmware/marvin/`)

**I2C Configuration:**
- Instance: FLEXCOM6 (TWI/Two-Wire Interface)
- Speed: 400 kHz (DRV_I2C_CLOCK_SPEED_IDX0 = 400000)
- Config location: `/default/src/config/default/configuration.h:102`, `/default/src/config/default/initialization.c`
- Pin assignment via FLEXCOM6_IO0/IO1 (R4/R2 on connector)

**CSI/ISC Peripherals:**
- CSI driver enabled: `/default/src/config/default/vision/drivers/csi/`
- ISC driver enabled: `/default/src/config/default/vision/drivers/isc/`
- CSI2DC bridge available: `/default/src/config/default/vision/drivers/csi2dc/`
- ISC configured for MIPI CSI-2 input with RGB input (ISC_ENABLE_MIPI_INTERFACE = true)

**GPIOs Available:**
- CAMERA_RESET: PC19 (pin G3, output, active-high)
- CAMERA_PWD: PC15 (pin E3, output, active-low)
- Both defined in `/default/src/config/default/pin_configurations.csv`
- Abundant "Available" pins for additional TC358743 INT signal

**Driver Structure:**
- Pattern: `/default/src/config/default/driver/i2c/drv_i2c.*` (driver layer)
- Vision drivers: `/default/src/config/default/vision/drivers/{csi|isc|csi2dc}/plib_*.c/h` and `drv_*.c/h`
- App-level code: `/default/src/app.c` (currently minimal; state machine scaffold)
- **Reusable pattern:** plib (peripheral lib) + drv (driver wrapper) architecture

**Harmony Version:** v5.6.4 (SAM9X7 DFP 1.9.170, vision v3.2.1)

---

### **2) Emirror Project** (`/Users/gregmrozek/Projects/microchip/guitar-pic/firmware/sam9x75_curiosity_emirror/`)

**Bridge/Sensor Drivers:**
- No TC358743 or TC358840 bridge chip
- Image sensors only: IMX219 (MIPI CSI-2 native), OV5640, OV2640, OV5647
- Sensor driver: `/src/config/default/vision/drivers/image_sensor/drv_image_sensor.{c|h}`
- Sensor implementations: `/src/config/default/vision/image_sensors/{imx219|ov5640|...}/`

**CSI/ISC Pipeline:**
- Libcamera abstraction layer: `/src/config/default/vision/libcamera/camera.{c|h}`
- CAMERA_configure() initializes ISC and CSI via DRV_ISC_OBJ and DRV_CSI_OBJ
- ISC callback chains to application via CAMERA_Register_CallBack()
- Frame buffers allocated: 1920×1080×4×DMA_MAX_BUFFERS in `.region_cache`

**Sensor I2C Programming:**
- Register table format: `DRV_IMAGE_SENSOR_REG` (struct: regAddr, regValue)
- Tables stored as const arrays (e.g., `imx219_raw_vga[]`, `ov5640_raw_qvga[]`)
- 0xFFFF terminator marks end; 0xFFFF values trigger wait/delay
- I2C modes: REG_BYTE_DATA_BYTE, REG_2BYTE_DATA_BYTE, REG_BYTE_DATA_2BYTE

**Reusable for TC358743:**
- Adapt `drv_image_sensor.{c|h}` pattern for bridge chip (register table, I2C probe, chip ID detection)
- Use libcamera abstraction layer as model for initialization sequencing
- Leverage CSI/ISC driver stubs already present in marvin

**Harmony Version:** v5.6.4 (identical to marvin)

---

**Key Finding:** Both projects share Harmony v5.6.4 + SAM9X7 DFP. Emirror's libcamera/sensor driver structure is ideal template for TC358743; marvin has I2C + ISC/CSI already configured and waiting for sensor/bridge driver attachment.
```

71	            CAMERA_Flip(sysObj.devCamera, 1);

85	/* Event filter for manual gauge control */
86	static leBool CamWindowMove_filterEvent(leWidget* target, leWidgetEvent* evt, void* data) {
87	    static lePoint lastPnt;
88	    leBool retval = LE_FALSE;
89	    lePoint pnt;
90	
91	    pnt.x = ((leWidgetEvent_TouchDown *) evt)->x;
92	    pnt.y = ((leWidgetEvent_TouchDown *) evt)->y;
93	
94	    switch (evt->id) {
95	            /* touch down and move events */
96	        case LE_EVENT_TOUCH_MOVE:
97	        case LE_EVENT_TOUCH_DOWN:
98	        {
99	            evt->accepted = LE_TRUE;
100	            evt->owner = target;
101	            /* touch in map area */
102	            if (pnt.y > 60 && pnt.y <= 480) {
103	                int xpos, ypos;
104	
105	                gfxcGetWindowPosition(ISC_CANVAS_ID, &xpos, &ypos);
106	
107	                xpos += (pnt.x - lastPnt.x);
108	                ypos += (pnt.y - lastPnt.y);
109	
110	                if ((xpos >= -480 && xpos <= 0) &&
111	                    (ypos >= -240 && ypos <= 0)) {
112	                    gfxcSetWindowPosition(ISC_CANVAS_ID, xpos, ypos);
113	                    gfxcCanvasUpdate(ISC_CANVAS_ID);
114	                }
115	                lastPnt.x = pnt.x;
116	                lastPnt.y = pnt.y;
117	            }
118	            retval = LE_TRUE;
119	            break;
120	        }
121	            /* Nothing to do on touch up events */
122	        case LE_EVENT_TOUCH_UP:
123	        {
124	            evt->accepted = LE_TRUE;
125	            retval = LE_TRUE;
126	            break;
127	        }
128	        default:
129	            break;
130	    }
131	    return retval;
132	}

## Survey Report: TC358743 HDMI-to-CSI-2 Bridge Driver for MPLAB Harmony SAM9X75

### **1) Marvin Project** (`/Users/gregmrozek/Projects/microchip/guitar-pic/firmware/marvin/`)

**I2C Configuration:**
- Instance: FLEXCOM6 (TWI/Two-Wire Interface)
- Speed: 400 kHz (DRV_I2C_CLOCK_SPEED_IDX0 = 400000)
- Config location: `/default/src/config/default/configuration.h:102`, `/default/src/config/default/initialization.c`
- Pin assignment via FLEXCOM6_IO0/IO1 (R4/R2 on connector)

**CSI/ISC Peripherals:**
- CSI driver enabled: `/default/src/config/default/vision/drivers/csi/`
- ISC driver enabled: `/default/src/config/default/vision/drivers/isc/`
- CSI2DC bridge available: `/default/src/config/default/vision/drivers/csi2dc/`
- ISC configured for MIPI CSI-2 input with RGB input (ISC_ENABLE_MIPI_INTERFACE = true)

**GPIOs Available:**
- CAMERA_RESET: PC19 (pin G3, output, active-high)
- CAMERA_PWD: PC15 (pin E3, output, active-low)
- Both defined in `/default/src/config/default/pin_configurations.csv`
- Abundant "Available" pins for additional TC358743 INT signal

**Driver Structure:**
- Pattern: `/default/src/config/default/driver/i2c/drv_i2c.*` (driver layer)
- Vision drivers: `/default/src/config/default/vision/drivers/{csi|isc|csi2dc}/plib_*.c/h` and `drv_*.c/h`
- App-level code: `/default/src/app.c` (currently minimal; state machine scaffold)
- **Reusable pattern:** plib (peripheral lib) + drv (driver wrapper) architecture

**Harmony Version:** v5.6.4 (SAM9X7 DFP 1.9.170, vision v3.2.1)

---

### **2) Emirror Project** (`/Users/gregmrozek/Projects/microchip/guitar-pic/firmware/sam9x75_curiosity_emirror/`)

**Bridge/Sensor Drivers:**
- No TC358743 or TC358840 bridge chip
- Image sensors only: IMX219 (MIPI CSI-2 native), OV5640, OV2640, OV5647
- Sensor driver: `/src/config/default/vision/drivers/image_sensor/drv_image_sensor.{c|h}`
- Sensor implementations: `/src/config/default/vision/image_sensors/{imx219|ov5640|...}/`

**CSI/ISC Pipeline:**
- Libcamera abstraction layer: `/src/config/default/vision/libcamera/camera.{c|h}`
- CAMERA_configure() initializes ISC and CSI via DRV_ISC_OBJ and DRV_CSI_OBJ
- ISC callback chains to application via CAMERA_Register_CallBack()
- Frame buffers allocated: 1920×1080×4×DMA_MAX_BUFFERS in `.region_cache`

**Sensor I2C Programming:**
- Register table format: `DRV_IMAGE_SENSOR_REG` (struct: regAddr, regValue)
- Tables stored as const arrays (e.g., `imx219_raw_vga[]`, `ov5640_raw_qvga[]`)
- 0xFFFF terminator marks end; 0xFFFF values trigger wait/delay
- I2C modes: REG_BYTE_DATA_BYTE, REG_2BYTE_DATA_BYTE, REG_BYTE_DATA_2BYTE

**Reusable for TC358743:**
- Adapt `drv_image_sensor.{c|h}` pattern for bridge chip (register table, I2C probe, chip ID detection)
- Use libcamera abstraction layer as model for initialization sequencing
- Leverage CSI/ISC driver stubs already present in marvin

**Harmony Version:** v5.6.4 (identical to marvin)

---

**Key Finding:** Both projects share Harmony v5.6.4 + SAM9X7 DFP. Emirror's libcamera/sensor driver structure is ideal template for TC358743; marvin has I2C + ISC/CSI already configured and waiting for sensor/bridge driver attachment.

**Which Waveshare TC358743 board do you have?**

Options:
- **HDMI to CSI-2 Adapter v1/v2** - The common Pi-style board with 15-pin FFC CSI connector, 27 MHz XTAL, I2C address 0x0F. Usually 2-lane CSI output.
- **HDMI to CSI-2 (B) / 4-lane variant** - Larger board, 4-lane CSI, often used with Jetson. Different I2C address possible.
- **Not sure / different board** - I'll check the silkscreen / datasheet and tell you.

**How should the TC358743 driver slot into the existing code?**

Options:
- **Pretend it's a sensor (Recommended)** - Port emirror's drv_image_sensor framework, add a 'tc358743' entry alongside imx219/ov5640. Reuses libcamera abstraction. Least new code.
- **Standalone drv_hdmi_bridge module** - Dedicated module in default/src/, called directly from app.c. Cleaner separation, since a bridge chip isn't really a sensor (no exposure, gain, etc.), but more new code.
- **Decide once we see the register sequence** - Start with probe/chip-ID code in a throwaway location; revisit the structure once we know how complex init and runtime handling will be.

**What should we base the TC358743 init/register sequences on?**

Options:
- **Mainline Linux driver + community 480p dumps** - Port logic from drivers/media/i2c/tc358743.c (correct state machine, EDID, IRQ handling) but use community/Waveshare 480p60 register tables for the actual values. Safest.
- **Toshiba reference code / app note only** - Use Toshiba's TC358743XBG reference initialization code if you have it. Closest to vendor intent but often incomplete for non-1080p inputs.
- **Start from a known-working 480p60 register dump** - Grab a working sequence (e.g., from a Pi user's tc358743.ko modparams or raspivid config) and hand-tune. Fastest path to first frame, least robust.


**Answer:** HDMI to CSI-2 Adapter v1/v2, Decide once we see the register sequence, Mainline Linux driver + community 480p dumps

Here's my proposed phased plan. Nothing to commit to yet — let's walk through it and adjust.

---

## Plan: TC358743 driver for marvin

### Phase 0 — Resolve open hardware/config questions (no code)

Before writing anything, confirm:
- **TC358743 I2C address on Waveshare v1/v2**: should be `0x0F` (7-bit). Verify by pullup on I2C_ADDR pin on the board's schematic.
- **Wii 5 V detect**: TC358743 needs source-side 5 V on its HDMI connector to start its HPD/EDID handshake. ElectronWarp → HDMI should provide this; worth confirming with a multimeter before we blame software.
- **ISC pixel format**: which Harmony ISC input format is currently configured — YUV422 8-bit, RGB888, or RAW. TC358743 can output any of those; we need to match.
- **TC358743 REFCLK**: Waveshare v1/v2 uses a 27 MHz XTAL on the board. Important for the PLL constants in Phase 3.
- **Pins**: confirm CAMERA_RESET (PC19) wires to the Waveshare board's RESET; decide whether we need its INT pin (optional — we can poll initially).

### Phase 1 — I2C probe & chip ID (one small file, throwaway-friendly)

Smallest possible code that proves I2C + reset work:
- Drive `CAMERA_RESET` through its reset pulse (≥10 µs low after power stable, then ≥500 µs delay).
- Read register `0x0000` (CHIPID) — expect `0x00 0x47`.
- Print via the debug UART set up in `28af4e4`.

If this reads back `0x0047`, we know: I2C wiring, I2C address, reset timing, and our transaction helpers all work.

### Phase 2 — Register access helpers

TC358743 has 16-bit register addresses and mixed 8/16/32-bit data widths. Emirror's `drv_image_sensor` helpers only handle 8/16-bit addr + byte or 2-byte data, so they won't cover us. Port the Linux driver's `i2c_wr8/wr16/wr32` and `i2c_rd8/rd16/rd32` against FLEXCOM6 TWI — it's a direct map.

### Phase 3 — Initialization sequence

Port from Linux `tc358743_initial_setup()` and friends in [tc358743.c](../linux-at91/drivers/media/i2c/tc358743.c):
- Software reset
- `SYS_CTRL` clock muxing (depends on REFCLK = 27 MHz)
- HDMI PHY config
- CSI-TX PLL + D-PHY timing (the Linux driver computes these from a `tc_data` struct — we'll hardcode for 2-lane 480p60)
- EDID RAM load (copy the 256-byte blob the Linux driver ships; it advertises 1080p/720p/480p)
- Enable HDMI input-format detection

This is where "throwaway file" becomes a real module. Good checkpoint to revisit the earlier integration question (sensor framework vs standalone).

### Phase 4 — Format detection & start CSI streaming

- Poll (or IRQ on TC358743's INT pin) the HDMI SYS_STATUS register until source lock and format match expectations.
- Program CSI-TX output timing for 480p60 in the chosen format.
- Release the CSI-TX stop state → pixel data flows.

### Phase 5 — Hook into marvin's ISC/CSI capture

- Call `tc358743_start()` after `SYS_Initialize()`.
- Arm ISC DMA into a framebuffer in SDRAM.
- Verify via the ISC frame-complete IRQ or frame counter that frames are landing.

### Phase 6 — First rendered frame

- Display the captured buffer on the Legato surface you already have running. Tune format/stride mismatches here.

---

### Risks I want on your radar

1. **Minimum CSI-TX bitrate.** TC358743's CSI-TX PLL has a minimum output rate; at 480p60 the native pixel rate is low enough that the Linux driver often has to run CSI-TX faster than the source and pad with blanking. We'll likely inherit that, and the SAM9X75 ISC has to tolerate it.
2. **TC358743 → ISC handshake.** SAM9X75 ISC expects a `Frame Start` + `Frame End` convention on CSI-2 that matches what TC358743 emits. Usually fine, but format tag mismatches (e.g. YUV422 8-bit vs 10-bit) will manifest as "no frames" and are painful to debug.
3. **EDID.** If the Wii sees a bad/missing EDID, it may fall back to 480i or refuse to output — check with the source before blaming the driver.

---

# marvin — Working Journal

Running log of planning, decisions, open questions, and work-in-progress for the marvin firmware. Newest entries at the top.

---

## Project north star

Vision-based guitar-playing robot. The marvin firmware captures live HDMI video from a Nintendo Wii (Guitar Hero / Rock Band), runs vision on it, and drives actuators to fret and strum a real guitar.

- **Target:** SAM9X75 Curiosity (MPLAB Harmony v5.6.4, SAM9X7 DFP 1.9.170, vision v3.2.1)
- **Video source:** Wii → ElectronWarp (component → HDMI, 480p60) → Waveshare HDMI-to-CSI-2 adapter (TC358743) → SAM9X75 MIPI CSI-2 RX → ISC → SDRAM
- **Display:** Legato GUI (already showing a basic screen as of commit `3bb441a`)

---

## Current focus

**TC358743 HDMI-to-CSI-2 bridge driver** — first real driver work on marvin. The bridge is the gate between "we have hardware wired up" and "we have pixels in memory."

### Hardware context

- **Bridge board:** Waveshare HDMI to CSI-2 Adapter v1/v2 (2-lane CSI, 27 MHz on-board XTAL, expected I2C address `0x0F`).
- **Source chain:** Wii → ElectronWarp (https://electron-shepherd.com/collections/all/products/electronwarp) → HDMI 480p60 → Waveshare → CSI-2 → SAM9X75.
- **Marvin pre-existing scaffolding:**
  - I2C: FLEXCOM6 @ 400 kHz (see `default/src/config/default/configuration.h:102`)
  - CSI driver: `default/src/config/default/vision/drivers/csi/` — configured for 2 data lanes (`CSI_NUM_LANES = CSI_DATA_LANES_2`, `configuration.h:167`)
  - ISC driver: `default/src/config/default/vision/drivers/isc/` — `enableMIPI = true`
  - CSI2DC bridge driver present
  - GPIOs: `CAMERA_RESET` = PC19 (active-high), `CAMERA_PWD` = PC15 (active-low), defined in `default/src/config/default/pin_configurations.csv`

### Reference sources (agreed)

- **Primary:** mainline Linux driver at `../linux-at91/drivers/media/i2c/tc358743.c` (2385 LOC) + `tc358743_regs.h` (782 LOC) + `include/media/i2c/tc358743.h`.
- **Secondary:** community / Waveshare 480p60 register dumps for the actual initialization values.
- **Emirror project** (`firmware/sam9x75_curiosity_emirror/`) as a template for how a camera-ish driver integrates with Harmony's ISC/CSI — NOT as a register reference (it drives IMX219/OV5640/OV2640/OV5647, no bridge chip).

### Integration approach — DEFERRED

Three options on the table:

1. Pretend TC358743 is a sensor — port emirror's `drv_image_sensor` framework and add a `tc358743` entry alongside IMX219/OV5640. Least new code; reuses libcamera abstraction.
2. Standalone `drv_hdmi_bridge` module. Cleaner semantically (a bridge isn't a sensor — no exposure, gain, AE/AWB), but more new code.
3. **Chosen:** Start probe/chip-ID code in a throwaway location, revisit once we see how complex init and runtime handling actually are.

### Phased plan

#### Phase 0 — Resolve open hardware/config questions (no code)

- [ ] Confirm TC358743 I2C address on Waveshare v1/v2 (expected `0x0F`, verify from schematic or by bus scan).
- [ ] Confirm Wii → ElectronWarp → Waveshare actually asserts HDMI 5 V on the bridge side (TC358743 needs it for HPD/EDID).
- [ ] Identify what pixel format the marvin ISC is currently configured for (YUV422 8-bit? RGB888? RAW?). TC358743 can output any of these; we must match.
- [ ] Confirm Waveshare v1/v2 REFCLK frequency (expected 27 MHz) — drives the PLL constants in Phase 3.
- [ ] Confirm `CAMERA_RESET` (PC19) physically wires to the Waveshare RESET pin. Decide whether to also use Waveshare's INT output (optional — polling works for bring-up).

#### Phase 1 — I2C probe & chip ID

Smallest code that proves I2C + reset work:

- Drive `CAMERA_RESET` through its reset pulse (≥10 µs low after power stable, then ≥500 µs wait).
- I2C read register `0x0000` (CHIPID), 16-bit address / 2-byte data → expect `0x00 0x47`.
- Print via the debug UART (wired up in commit `28af4e4`).

Exit criteria: we read `0x0047` back from a power-cycled board.

#### Phase 2 — Register access helpers

TC358743 has 16-bit register addresses and mixed 8/16/32-bit data widths. Emirror's sensor helpers only cover 8/16-bit addr + byte / 2-byte data — not enough. Port the Linux driver's `i2c_wr8/wr16/wr32` + `i2c_rd8/rd16/rd32` against FLEXCOM6 TWI. Direct map from the kernel driver.

#### Phase 3 — Initialization sequence

Port from Linux `tc358743_initial_setup()` and its callees:

- Software reset
- `SYS_CTRL` clock muxing (depends on 27 MHz REFCLK)
- HDMI PHY config
- CSI-TX PLL + D-PHY timing (Linux driver computes from a `tc_data` struct — we hardcode for 2-lane 480p60)
- EDID RAM load (copy the 256-byte blob from the Linux driver; advertises 1080p/720p/480p)
- Enable HDMI input-format detection

This is the point where "throwaway file" becomes a real module. Revisit integration question (sensor framework vs standalone) here.

#### Phase 4 — Format detection & start CSI streaming

- Poll (or IRQ on TC358743's INT pin) the HDMI SYS_STATUS register until source is locked and the format matches expectation.
- Program CSI-TX output for 480p60 in the chosen pixel format.
- Release CSI-TX stop state → pixel data flows.

#### Phase 5 — Hook into marvin's ISC/CSI capture

- Call `tc358743_start()` after `SYS_Initialize()`.
- Arm ISC DMA into a framebuffer in SDRAM.
- Verify via ISC frame-complete IRQ / frame counter that frames are landing.

#### Phase 6 — First rendered frame

- Display the captured buffer on the existing Legato surface. Fix format/stride mismatches here.

### Known risks

1. **TC358743 CSI-TX minimum bitrate.** At 480p60 the native pixel rate is low enough that the Linux driver runs CSI-TX faster than the source and pads with blanking. We'll likely inherit that approach, and SAM9X75 ISC must tolerate it.
2. **ISC ↔ TC358743 handshake.** ISC expects specific CSI-2 frame-start/frame-end conventions. Format tag mismatches (YUV422 8-bit vs 10-bit, etc.) manifest as "no frames" and are painful to debug.
3. **EDID.** If the Wii sees a bad/missing EDID it may fall back to 480i or refuse to output. Test the source independently before blaming the driver.

---

# Project rules

These rules apply to every session on this repo. Follow them without being reminded.

## Journals are the source of truth for planning and progress

This repo uses working journals to track planning, decisions, open questions, and work-in-progress *outside* the chat context so they survive across sessions, compactions, and restarts.

Current journals:

- `firmware/marvin/docs/journal.md` — marvin firmware (SAM9X75 vision-based guitar-playing robot)

When working on a subproject that has a journal:

1. **Read the journal first.** Before responding to any non-trivial request, read the journal for that subproject. It contains the current focus, phased plan, open questions, decision log, and session log — the state you need to be useful.
2. **Update the journal as you go.** When we make a decision, resolve an open question, finish a plan phase, or finish a session, reflect that in the journal. Newest entries at the top within each section.
   - Decisions → append to the decision log with date and rationale.
   - Resolved open questions → remove from "Open questions" and add to the decision log with the answer and rationale.
   - Plan progress → check off phase items; add sub-bullets for anything learned during implementation.
   - Session close → add a dated session-log entry summarizing what happened.
3. **Prefer updating the journal over restating plans in chat.** If I'd otherwise write a multi-paragraph plan in chat, it belongs in the journal — the chat is ephemeral, the journal isn't.
4. **If a new subproject needs a journal, create one** using the same structure as `firmware/marvin/docs/journal.md`, and add it to the list above in this file.

## Code comments describe current code only

Comments in source files explain **what the code currently does and why**, when that's non-obvious. They are not a development diary.

Do not put any of the following in source comments — they belong in the journal, commit messages, or PR descriptions:

- Narrative of how the code evolved ("previously we did X, now we do Y", "this replaces the old …")
- Debug notes, troubleshooting history, or why something *doesn't* work
- TODO lists for future features (use the journal or an issue tracker)
- References to tasks, tickets, or past conversations ("fix for Greg's bug", "see chat from 2026-05-01")
- Extensive block comments explaining design rationale — a one-line "why" is fine; multi-paragraph prose goes in the journal

**Default to no comment.** Only add one when removing it would confuse a future reader. If you catch yourself wanting to write a paragraph, write it in the journal instead and link from the code if needed (e.g. `// see firmware/marvin/docs/journal.md`).

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-01 13:44:08Z)**_

Strong finding on pixel format — marvin's pipeline is configured for **RGB888**, not YUV. From [configuration.h:112-180](firmware/marvin/default/src/config/default/configuration.h#L112):

- `ISC_INPUT_FORMAT_TYPE = DRV_IMAGE_SENSOR_RGB`, 8-bit
- `CSI_DATA_FORMAT_TYPE = CSI2_DATA_FORMAT_RGB888` (MIPI data type `0x24`)
- `CSI2DC_VIDEO_PIPE_FORMAT_TYPE = CSI2DC_DATA_FORMAT_RGB888`
- `ISC_OUTPUT_FORMAT_TYPE = ISC_RLP_CFG_MODE_ARGB32` (packed ARGB32 in SDRAM)

So the TC358743 must emit **RGB888 over CSI-2**. Noted: ISC still has Bayer-demosaic / white-balance / gamma / DPC enabled from MCC template defaults — those are Bayer-pipe only and will need to be disabled / bypassed for RGB input. I'll flag that as a follow-up open question.

Now let me confirm the Waveshare board specifics from reliable sources.

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-01 13:44:56Z)**_

Enough to close out the software questions. Key facts confirmed:

- Kernel driver restricts REFCLK to `26 MHz`, `27 MHz`, or `42 MHz` only ([tc358743.c:717-719](../linux-at91/drivers/media/i2c/tc358743.c#L717-L719)). Waveshare v1/v2 is 27 MHz (universally documented in Pi/Jetson community).
- The kernel's one in-tree DT example uses I2C address `0x0f` ([imx6q-h100.dts:190](../linux-at91/arch/arm/boot/dts/nxp/imx/imx6q-h100.dts#L190) — `tc358743@f`). Matches the Waveshare default.
- Register access helpers we need to port (for Phase 2): `i2c_rd/wr` + `i2c_rd8/wr8/rd16/wr16/rd32/wr32` exist at [tc358743.c:131-269](../linux-at91/drivers/media/i2c/tc358743.c#L131-L269). Clean direct port.

Let me update the journal with the resolved answers, the RGB888 finding, the new Bayer-pipeline follow-up, and the hardware questions that remain yours to answer.

| Register helper strategy | Direct port of kernel `i2c_rd/wr/rd8/wr8/rd16/wr16/rd32/wr32` family | Clean abstraction at [tc358743.c:131-269](../linux-at91/drivers/media/i2c/tc358743.c#L131-L269) |

### New open question uncovered

Marvin's MCC config has Bayer-only ISC blocks enabled (DPC, white balance, gamma, Bayer pattern) even though `ISC_INPUT_FORMAT_TYPE = RGB`. Inconsistent but probably harmless if `drv_isc.c` gates them on input format — needs a read during Phase 5.

### Remaining Phase 0 items — yours to answer

These need hardware you have and I don't:

1. **Is PC19 (`CAMERA_RESET`) actually wired to the Waveshare RESET pin** on your marvin carrier? Schematic check or continuity ping.
2. **Is TC358743 INT exposed to any SAM9X75 GPIO?** Usually no on the stock 15-pin FFC pinout — polling works fine for bring-up, just confirm.
3. **Bench check the source chain:** Wii → ElectronWarp → Waveshare →
   - (a) HDMI 5 V present on the Waveshare HDMI connector (multimeter)?
   - (b) Actually 480p60 out of ElectronWarp (plug into a TV that reports resolution)?

Once (1) is answered we're ready to drop into plan mode and start Phase 1 (I2C probe + chip-ID read). (2) and (3) can be done in parallel.

---

## Adding MCP Servers: Claude Code CLI vs VS Code

Here's how to add MCP servers in each environment:

### 1. Claude Code CLI

**Three transport options:**

```bash
# HTTP (recommended for remote servers)
claude mcp add --transport http notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp

# SSE (deprecated but available)
claude mcp add --transport sse asana https://mcp.asana.com/sse

# Stdio (local processes)
claude mcp add --transport stdio airtable --env AIRTABLE_API_KEY=YOUR_KEY \
  -- npx -y airtable-mcp-server
```

**Three scope options:**

```bash
# Local scope (default) — private to you, this project only
claude mcp add --transport http stripe https://mcp.stripe.com

# Project scope — shared via .mcp.json in version control
claude mcp add --transport http paypal --scope project https://mcp.paypal.com/mcp

# User scope — available across all your projects
claude mcp add --transport http hubspot --scope user https://mcp.hubspot.com
```

**Manage servers:**

```bash
claude mcp list                # List all configured servers
claude mcp get github          # View details for a server
claude mcp remove github       # Remove a server
claude mcp reset-project-choices  # Reset approvals for project-scoped servers
```

**Key details:**

- Options (`--transport`, `--env`, `--scope`, `--header`) come **before** the server name
- `--` separates options from the server command (stdio only)
- Scopes store configs in:
  - `local`: `~/.claude.json` (project-specific, private)
  - `project`: `.mcp.json` at project root (shared with team)
  - `user`: `~/.claude.json` (all projects, private)

### 2. VS Code Integration

**Within VS Code, you have two paths:**

**Path A: CLI in integrated terminal**

Open the integrated terminal (`` Ctrl+` `` / `` Cmd+` ``) and run the same `claude mcp add` commands above. Servers added via CLI are immediately available in the extension.

**Path B: Manage servers via `/mcp` in chat**

Once servers are configured (via CLI), you can manage them directly in the VS Code chat:

- Type `/mcp` in the prompt box → opens MCP management dialog
- Enable/disable servers
- Reconnect to a server
- Manage OAuth authentication

**How inheritance works:**

The VS Code extension and CLI share the same configuration files:
- Both read from `~/.claude/settings.json` (settings layer)
- Both read from `.mcp.json` (project scope)
- MCP servers configured in the CLI are **automatically available** in the extension (no separate VS Code configuration needed)

---

## Practical Example

Add a GitHub MCP server for code reviews:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http github https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/ \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_GITHUB_PAT" --scope project
```

This creates `.mcp.json` in your project root. Both CLI and VS Code extension now have access. In VS Code, type `/mcp` to toggle it on or manage authentication.

---

**Official documentation:**
- [MCP servers in Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md)
- [VS Code extension guide](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/vs-code.md) (search for "Connect to external tools with MCP")

171	              <p style={{
172	      margin: '0.5rem 0',
173	      fontSize: '0.9rem'
174	    }}>
175	                {server.description}
176	              </p>
177	
178	              {server.setupUrl && <p style={{
179	      margin: '0.25rem 0',
180	      fontSize: '0.8rem',
181	      fontStyle: 'italic',
182	      opacity: 0.7
183	    }}>
184	                  Requires user-specific URL.{' '}
185	                  <a href={server.setupUrl} style={{
186	      textDecoration: 'underline'
187	    }}>
188	                    Get your URL here
189	                  </a>.
190	                </p>}
191	
192	              {commandToShow && !server.setupUrl && <>
193	                <p style={{
194	      display: 'block',
195	      fontSize: '0.75rem',
196	      fontWeight: 500,
197	      minWidth: 'fit-content',
198	      marginTop: '0.5rem',
199	      marginBottom: 0
200	    }}>
201	                  {platform === "claudeCode" ? "Command" : "URL"}
202	                </p>

204	                  <code>
205	                    {commandToShow}
206	                  </code>
207	                </div>
208	              </>}
209	            </div>;
210	  })}
211	      </div>
212	    </>;
213	};
214	
215	Claude Code can connect to hundreds of external tools and data sources through the [Model Context Protocol (MCP)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/introduction), an open source standard for AI-tool integrations. MCP servers give Claude Code access to your tools, databases, and APIs.
216	
217	Connect a server when you find yourself copying data into chat from another tool, like an issue tracker or a monitoring dashboard. Once connected, Claude can read and act on that system directly instead of working from what you paste.
218	
219	## What you can do with MCP
220	
221	With MCP servers connected, you can ask Claude Code to:
222	
223	* **Implement features from issue trackers**: "Add the feature described in JIRA issue ENG-4521 and create a PR on GitHub."
224	* **Analyze monitoring data**: "Check Sentry and Statsig to check the usage of the feature described in ENG-4521."
225	* **Query databases**: "Find emails of 10 random users who used feature ENG-4521, based on our PostgreSQL database."
226	* **Integrate designs**: "Update our standard email template based on the new Figma designs that were posted in Slack"
227	* **Automate workflows**: "Create Gmail drafts inviting these 10 users to a feedback session about the new feature."
228	* **React to external events**: An MCP server can also act as a [channel](/en/channels) that pushes messages into your session, so Claude reacts to Telegram messages, Discord chats, or webhook events while you're away.
229	
230	## Popular MCP servers
231	
232	Here are some commonly used MCP servers you can connect to Claude Code:
233	
234	<Warning>
235	  Use third party MCP servers at your own risk - Anthropic has not verified
236	  the correctness or security of all these servers.
237	  Make sure you trust MCP servers you are installing.
238	  Be especially careful when using MCP servers that could fetch untrusted
239	  content, as these can expose you to prompt injection risk.
240	</Warning>
241	
242	<MCPServersTable platform="claudeCode" />
243	
244	<Note>
245	  **Need a specific integration?** [Find hundreds more MCP servers on GitHub](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers), or build your own using the [MCP SDK](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/quickstart/server).
246	</Note>
247	
248	## Installing MCP servers
249	
250	MCP servers can be configured in three different ways depending on your needs:
251	
252	### Option 1: Add a remote HTTP server
253	
254	HTTP servers are the recommended option for connecting to remote MCP servers. This is the most widely supported transport for cloud-based services.
255	
256	```bash theme={null}
257	# Basic syntax
258	claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url>
259	
260	# Real example: Connect to Notion
261	claude mcp add --transport http notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp
262	
263	# Example with Bearer token
264	claude mcp add --transport http secure-api https://api.example.com/mcp \
265	  --header "Authorization: Bearer your-token"
266	```
267	
268	### Option 2: Add a remote SSE server
269	
270	<Warning>
271	  The SSE (Server-Sent Events) transport is deprecated. Use HTTP servers instead, where available.
272	</Warning>
273	
274	```bash theme={null}
275	# Basic syntax
276	claude mcp add --transport sse <name> <url>
277	
278	# Real example: Connect to Asana
279	claude mcp add --transport sse asana https://mcp.asana.com/sse
280	
281	# Example with authentication header
282	claude mcp add --transport sse private-api https://api.company.com/sse \
283	  --header "X-API-Key: your-key-here"
284	```
285	
286	### Option 3: Add a local stdio server
287	
288	Stdio servers run as local processes on your machine. They're ideal for tools that need direct system access or custom scripts.
289	
290	```bash theme={null}
291	# Basic syntax
292	claude mcp add [options] <name> -- <command> [args...]
293	
294	# Real example: Add Airtable server
295	claude mcp add --transport stdio --env AIRTABLE_API_KEY=YOUR_KEY airtable \
296	  -- npx -y airtable-mcp-server
297	```
298	
299	<Note>
300	  **Important: Option ordering**
301	
302	  All options (`--transport`, `--env`, `--scope`, `--header`) must come **before** the server name. The `--` (double dash) then separates the server name from the command and arguments that get passed to the MCP server.
303	
304	  For example:
305	
306	  * `claude mcp add --transport stdio myserver -- npx server` → runs `npx server`
307	  * `claude mcp add --transport stdio --env KEY=value myserver -- python server.py --port 8080` → runs `python server.py --port 8080` with `KEY=value` in environment
308	
309	  This prevents conflicts between Claude's flags and the server's flags.
310	</Note>
311	
312	### Managing your servers
313	
314	Once configured, you can manage your MCP servers with these commands:
315	
316	```bash theme={null}
317	# List all configured servers
318	claude mcp list
319	
320	# Get details for a specific server
321	claude mcp get github
322	
323	# Remove a server
324	claude mcp remove github
325	
326	# (within Claude Code) Check server status
327	/mcp
328	```
329	
330	### Dynamic tool updates
331	
332	Claude Code supports MCP `list_changed` notifications, allowing MCP servers to dynamically update their available tools, prompts, and resources without requiring you to disconnect and reconnect. When an MCP server sends a `list_changed` notification, Claude Code automatically refreshes the available capabilities from that server.
333	
334	### Automatic reconnection
335	
336	If an HTTP or SSE server disconnects mid-session, Claude Code automatically reconnects with exponential backoff: up to five attempts, starting at a one-second delay and doubling each time. The server appears as pending in `/mcp` while reconnection is in progress. After five failed attempts the server is marked as failed and you can retry manually from `/mcp`. Stdio servers are local processes and are not reconnected automatically.
337	
338	The same backoff applies when an HTTP or SSE server fails its initial connection at startup. As of v2.1.121, Claude Code retries the initial connection up to three times on transient errors such as a 5xx response, a connection refused, or a timeout, then marks the server as failed if it still cannot connect. Authentication and not-found errors are not retried because they require a configuration change to resolve.
339	
340	### Push messages with channels
341	
342	An MCP server can also push messages directly into your session so Claude can react to external events like CI results, monitoring alerts, or chat messages. To enable this, your server declares the `claude/channel` capability and you opt it in with the `--channels` flag at startup. See [Channels](/en/channels) to use an officially supported channel, or [Channels reference](/en/channels-reference) to build your own.
343	
344	<Tip>
345	  Tips:
346	
347	  * Use the `--scope` flag to specify where the configuration is stored:
348	    * `local` (default): Available only to you in the current project (was called `project` in older versions)
349	    * `project`: Shared with everyone in the project via `.mcp.json` file
350	    * `user`: Available to you across all projects (was called `global` in older versions)
351	  * Set environment variables with `--env` flags (for example, `--env KEY=value`)
352	  * Configure MCP server startup timeout using the MCP\_TIMEOUT environment variable (for example, `MCP_TIMEOUT=10000 claude` sets a 10-second timeout)
353	  * Claude Code will display a warning when MCP tool output exceeds 10,000 tokens. To increase this limit, set the `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS` environment variable (for example, `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS=50000`)
354	  * Use `/mcp` to authenticate with remote servers that require OAuth 2.0 authentication
355	</Tip>
356	
357	### Plugin-provided MCP servers
358	
359	[Plugins](/en/plugins) can bundle MCP servers, automatically providing tools and integrations when the plugin is enabled. Plugin MCP servers work identically to user-configured servers.
360	
361	**How plugin MCP servers work**:
362	
363	* Plugins define MCP servers in `.mcp.json` at the plugin root or inline in `plugin.json`
364	* When a plugin is enabled, its MCP servers start automatically
365	* Plugin MCP tools appear alongside manually configured MCP tools
366	* Plugin servers are managed through plugin installation (not `/mcp` commands)
367	
368	**Example plugin MCP configuration**:
369	
370	In `.mcp.json` at plugin root:
371	
372	```json theme={null}
373	{
374	  "mcpServers": {
375	    "database-tools": {
376	      "command": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/servers/db-server",
377	      "args": ["--config", "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/config.json"],
378	      "env": {
379	        "DB_URL": "${DB_URL}"
380	      }
381	    }
382	  }
383	}
384	```
385	
386	Or inline in `plugin.json`:
387	
388	```json theme={null}
389	{
390	  "name": "my-plugin",
391	  "mcpServers": {
392	    "plugin-api": {
393	      "command": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/servers/api-server",
394	      "args": ["--port", "8080"]
395	    }
396	  }
397	}
398	```
399	
400	**Plugin MCP features**:
401	
402	* **Automatic lifecycle**: At session startup, servers for enabled plugins connect automatically. If you enable or disable a plugin during a session, run `/reload-plugins` to connect or disconnect its MCP servers
403	* **Environment variables**: use `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` for bundled plugin files and `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}` for [persistent state](/en/plugins-reference#persistent-data-directory) that survives plugin updates
404	* **User environment access**: Access to same environment variables as manually configured servers
405	* **Multiple transport types**: Support stdio, SSE, and HTTP transports (transport support may vary by server)
406	
407	**Viewing plugin MCP servers**:
408	
409	```bash theme={null}
410	# Within Claude Code, see all MCP servers including plugin ones
411	/mcp
412	```
413	
414	Plugin servers appear in the list with indicators showing they come from plugins.
415	
416	**Benefits of plugin MCP servers**:
417	
418	* **Bundled distribution**: Tools and servers packaged together
419	* **Automatic setup**: No manual MCP configuration needed
420	* **Team consistency**: Everyone gets the same tools when plugin is installed
421	
422	See the [plugin components reference](/en/plugins-reference#mcp-servers) for details on bundling MCP servers with plugins.
423	
424	## MCP installation scopes
425	
426	MCP servers can be configured at three scopes. The scope you choose controls which projects the server loads in and whether the configuration is shared with your team.
427	
428	| Scope                     | Loads in             | Shared with team         | Stored in                   |
429	| ------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------ | --------------------------- |
430	| [Local](#local-scope)     | Current project only | No                       | `~/.claude.json`            |
431	| [Project](#project-scope) | Current project only | Yes, via version control | `.mcp.json` in project root |
432	| [User](#user-scope)       | All your projects    | No                       | `~/.claude.json`            |
433	
434	### Local scope
435	
436	Local scope is the default. A local-scoped server loads only in the project where you added it and stays private to you. Claude Code stores it in `~/.claude.json` under that project's path, so the same server won't appear in your other projects. Use local scope for personal development servers, experimental configurations, or servers with credentials you don't want in version control.
437	
438	<Note>
439	  The term "local scope" for MCP servers differs from general local settings. MCP local-scoped servers are stored in `~/.claude.json` (your home directory), while general local settings use `.claude/settings.local.json` (in the project directory). See [Settings](/en/settings#settings-files) for details on settings file locations.
440	</Note>
441	
442	```bash theme={null}
443	# Add a local-scoped server (default)
444	claude mcp add --transport http stripe https://mcp.stripe.com
445	
446	# Explicitly specify local scope
447	claude mcp add --transport http stripe --scope local https://mcp.stripe.com
448	```
449	
450	The command writes the server into the entry for your current project inside `~/.claude.json`. The example below shows the result when you run it from `/path/to/your/project`:
451	
452	```json theme={null}
453	{
454	  "projects": {
455	    "/path/to/your/project": {
456	      "mcpServers": {
457	        "stripe": {
458	          "type": "http",
459	          "url": "https://mcp.stripe.com"
460	        }
461	      }
462	    }
463	  }
464	}
465	```
466	
467	### Project scope
468	
469	Project-scoped servers enable team collaboration by storing configurations in a `.mcp.json` file at your project's root directory. This file is designed to be checked into version control, ensuring all team members have access to the same MCP tools and services. When you add a project-scoped server, Claude Code automatically creates or updates this file with the appropriate configuration structure.
470	
471	```bash theme={null}
472	# Add a project-scoped server
473	claude mcp add --transport http paypal --scope project https://mcp.paypal.com/mcp
474	```
475	
476	The resulting `.mcp.json` file follows a standardized format:
477	
478	```json theme={null}
479	{
480	  "mcpServers": {
481	    "shared-server": {
482	      "command": "/path/to/server",
483	      "args": [],
484	      "env": {}
485	    }
486	  }
487	}
488	```
489	
490	For security reasons, Claude Code prompts for approval before using project-scoped servers from `.mcp.json` files. If you need to reset these approval choices, use the `claude mcp reset-project-choices` command.
491	
492	### User scope
493	
494	User-scoped servers are stored in `~/.claude.json` and provide cross-project accessibility, making them available across all projects on your machine while remaining private to your user account. This scope works well for personal utility servers, development tools, or services you frequently use across different projects.
495	
496	```bash theme={null}
497	# Add a user server
498	claude mcp add --transport http hubspot --scope user https://mcp.hubspot.com/anthropic
499	```
500
```
