# Use Claude Code in VS Code

> Install and configure the Claude Code extension for VS Code. Get AI coding assistance with inline diffs, @-mentions, plan review, and keyboard shortcuts.

<img src="https://mintcdn.com/claude-code/-YhHHmtSxwr7W8gy/images/vs-code-extension-interface.jpg?fit=max&auto=format&n=-YhHHmtSxwr7W8gy&q=85&s=300652d5678c63905e6b0ea9e50835f8" alt="VS Code editor with the Claude Code extension panel open on the right side, showing a conversation with Claude" width="2500" height="1155" data-path="images/vs-code-extension-interface.jpg" />

The VS Code extension provides a native graphical interface for Claude Code, integrated directly into your IDE. This is the recommended way to use Claude Code in VS Code.

With the extension, you can review and edit Claude's plans before accepting them, auto-accept edits as they're made, @-mention files with specific line ranges from your selection, access conversation history, and open multiple conversations in separate tabs or windows.

## Prerequisites

Before installing, make sure you have:

* VS Code 1.98.0 or higher
* An Anthropic account (you'll sign in when you first open the extension). If you're using a third-party provider like Amazon Bedrock or Google Vertex AI, see [Use third-party providers](#use-third-party-providers) instead.

<Tip>
  The extension includes the CLI (command-line interface), which you can access from VS Code's integrated terminal for advanced features. See [VS Code extension vs. Claude Code CLI](#vs-code-extension-vs-claude-code-cli) for details.
</Tip>

## Install the extension

Click the link for your IDE to install directly:

* [Install for VS Code](vscode:extension/anthropic.claude-code)
* [Install for Cursor](cursor:extension/anthropic.claude-code)

Or in VS Code, press `Cmd+Shift+X` (Mac) or `Ctrl+Shift+X` (Windows/Linux) to open the Extensions view, search for "Claude Code", and click **Install**.

<Note>If the extension doesn't appear after installation, restart VS Code or run "Developer: Reload Window" from the Command Palette.</Note>

## Get started

Once installed, you can start using Claude Code through the VS Code interface:

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open the Claude Code panel">
    Throughout VS Code, the Spark icon indicates Claude Code: <img src="https://mintcdn.com/claude-code/c5r9_6tjPMzFdDDT/images/vs-code-spark-icon.svg?fit=max&auto=format&n=c5r9_6tjPMzFdDDT&q=85&s=3ca45e00deadec8c8f4b4f807da94505" alt="Spark icon" style={{display: "inline", height: "0.85em", verticalAlign: "middle"}} width="16" height="16" data-path="images/vs-code-spark-icon.svg" />

    The quickest way to open Claude is to click the Spark icon in the **Editor Toolbar** (top-right corner of the editor). The icon only appears when you have a file open.

    <img src="https://mintcdn.com/claude-code/mfM-EyoZGnQv8JTc/images/vs-code-editor-icon.png?fit=max&auto=format&n=mfM-EyoZGnQv8JTc&q=85&s=eb4540325d94664c51776dbbfec4cf02" alt="VS Code editor showing the Spark icon in the Editor Toolbar" width="2796" height="734" data-path="images/vs-code-editor-icon.png" />

    Other ways to open Claude Code:

    * **Activity Bar**: click the Spark icon in the left sidebar to open the sessions list. Click any session to open it as a full editor tab, or start a new one. This icon is always visible in the Activity Bar.
    * **Command Palette**: `Cmd+Shift+P` (Mac) or `Ctrl+Shift+P` (Windows/Linux), type "Claude Code", and select an option like "Open in New Tab"
    * **Status Bar**: click **✱ Claude Code** in the bottom-right corner of the window. This works even when no file is open.

    You can drag the Claude panel to reposition it anywhere in VS Code. See [Customize your workflow](#customize-your-workflow) for details.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Sign in">
    The first time you open the panel, a sign-in screen appears. Click **Sign in** and complete authorization in your browser.

    If you see **Not logged in · Please run /login** later, the extension reopens the sign-in screen automatically. If it doesn't appear, reload the window from the Command Palette with **Developer: Reload Window**.

    If you have `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` set in your shell but still see the sign-in prompt, VS Code may not have inherited your shell environment. Launch VS Code from a terminal with `code .` so it inherits your environment variables, or sign in with your Claude account instead.

    After you sign in, a **Learn Claude Code** checklist appears. Work through each item by clicking **Show me**, or dismiss it with the X. To reopen it later, uncheck **Hide Onboarding** in VS Code settings under Extensions → Claude Code.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Send a prompt">
    Ask Claude to help with your code or files, whether that's explaining how something works, debugging an issue, or making changes.

    <Tip>Claude automatically sees your selected text. Press `Option+K` (Mac) / `Alt+K` (Windows/Linux) to also insert an @-mention reference (like `@file.ts#5-10`) into your prompt.</Tip>

    Here's an example of asking about a particular line in a file:

    <img src="https://mintcdn.com/claude-code/FVYz38sRY-VuoGHA/images/vs-code-send-prompt.png?fit=max&auto=format&n=FVYz38sRY-VuoGHA&q=85&s=ede3ed8d8d5f940e01c5de636d009cfd" alt="VS Code editor with lines 2-3 selected in a Python file, and the Claude Code panel showing a question about those lines with an @-mention reference" width="3288" height="1876" data-path="images/vs-code-send-prompt.png" />
  </Step>

  <Step title="Review changes">
    When Claude wants to edit a file, it shows a side-by-side comparison of the original and proposed changes, then asks for permission. You can accept, reject, or tell Claude what to do instead. If you edit the proposed content directly in the diff view before accepting, Claude is told that you modified it so it does not assume the file matches its original proposal.

    <img src="https://mintcdn.com/claude-code/FVYz38sRY-VuoGHA/images/vs-code-edits.png?fit=max&auto=format&n=FVYz38sRY-VuoGHA&q=85&s=e005f9b41c541c5c7c59c082f7c4841c" alt="VS Code showing a diff of Claude's proposed changes with a permission prompt asking whether to make the edit" width="3292" height="1876" data-path="images/vs-code-edits.png" />
  </Step>
</Steps>

For more ideas on what you can do with Claude Code, see [Common workflows](/en/common-workflows).

<Tip>
  Run "Claude Code: Open Walkthrough" from the Command Palette for a guided tour of the basics.
</Tip>

## Use the prompt box

The prompt box supports several features:

* **Permission modes**: click the mode indicator at the bottom of the prompt box to switch modes. In normal mode, Claude asks permission before each action. In Plan mode, Claude describes what it will do and waits for approval before making changes. VS Code automatically opens the plan as a full markdown document where you can add inline comments to give feedback before Claude begins. In auto-accept mode, Claude makes edits without asking. Set the default in VS Code settings under `claudeCode.initialPermissionMode`.
* **Command menu**: click `/` or type `/` to open the command menu. Options include attaching files, switching models, toggling extended thinking, viewing plan usage (`/usage`), and starting a [Remote Control](/en/remote-control) session (`/remote-control`). The Customize section provides access to MCP servers, hooks, memory, permissions, and plugins. Items with a terminal icon open in the integrated terminal.
* **Context indicator**: the prompt box shows how much of Claude's context window you're using. Claude automatically compacts when needed, or you can run `/compact` manually.
* **Extended thinking**: lets Claude spend more time reasoning through complex problems. Toggle it on via the command menu (`/`). Claude's reasoning appears in the conversation as collapsed blocks: click a block to read it, or press `Ctrl+O` to expand or collapse every thinking block in the session. See [Extended thinking](/en/common-workflows#use-extended-thinking-thinking-mode) for details.
* **Multi-line input**: press `Shift+Enter` to add a new line without sending. This also works in the "Other" free-text input of question dialogs.

### Reference files and folders

Use @-mentions to give Claude context about specific files or folders. When you type `@` followed by a file or folder name, Claude reads that content and can answer questions about it or make changes to it. Claude Code supports fuzzy matching, so you can type partial names to find what you need:

```text theme={null}
> Explain the logic in @auth (fuzzy matches auth.js, AuthService.ts, etc.)
> What's in @src/components/ (include a trailing slash for folders)
```

For large PDFs, you can ask Claude to read specific pages instead of the whole file: a single page, a range like pages 1-10, or an open-ended range like page 3 onward.

When you select text in the editor, Claude can see your highlighted code automatically. The prompt box footer shows how many lines are selected. Press `Option+K` (Mac) / `Alt+K` (Windows/Linux) to insert an @-mention with the file path and line numbers (e.g., `@app.ts#5-10`). Click the selection indicator to toggle whether Claude can see your highlighted text - the eye-slash icon means the selection is hidden from Claude.

You can also hold `Shift` while dragging files into the prompt box to add them as attachments. Click the X on any attachment to remove it from context.

### Resume past conversations

Click the **Session history** button at the top of the Claude Code panel to access your conversation history. You can search by keyword or browse by time (Today, Yesterday, Last 7 days, etc.). Click any conversation to resume it with the full message history. New sessions receive AI-generated titles based on your first message. Hover over a session to reveal rename and remove actions: rename to give it a descriptive title, or remove to delete it from the list. For more on resuming sessions, see [Common workflows](/en/common-workflows#resume-previous-conversations).

### Resume remote sessions from Claude.ai

If you use [Claude Code on the web](/en/claude-code-on-the-web), you can resume those remote sessions directly in VS Code. This requires signing in with **Claude.ai Subscription**, not Anthropic Console.

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open session history">
    Click the **Session history** button at the top of the Claude Code panel.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Select the Remote tab">
    The dialog shows two tabs: Local and Remote. Click **Remote** to see sessions from claude.ai.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Select a session to resume">
    Browse or search your remote sessions. Click any session to download it and continue the conversation locally.
  </Step>
</Steps>

<Note>
  Only web sessions started with a GitHub repository appear in the Remote tab. Resuming loads the conversation history locally; changes are not synced back to claude.ai.
</Note>

## Customize your workflow

Once you're up and running, you can reposition the Claude panel, run multiple sessions, or switch to terminal mode.

### Choose where Claude lives

You can drag the Claude panel to reposition it anywhere in VS Code. Grab the panel's tab or title bar and drag it to:

* **Secondary sidebar**: the right side of the window. Keeps Claude visible while you code.
* **Primary sidebar**: the left sidebar with icons for Explorer, Search, etc.
* **Editor area**: opens Claude as a tab alongside your files. Useful for side tasks.

<Tip>
  Use the sidebar for your main Claude session and open additional tabs for side tasks. Claude remembers your preferred location. The Activity Bar sessions list icon is separate from the Claude panel: the sessions list is always visible in the Activity Bar, while the Claude panel icon only appears there when the panel is docked to the left sidebar.
</Tip>

### Run multiple conversations

Use **Open in New Tab** or **Open in New Window** from the Command Palette to start additional conversations. Each conversation maintains its own history and context, allowing you to work on different tasks in parallel.

When using tabs, a small colored dot on the spark icon indicates status: blue means a permission request is pending, orange means Claude finished while the tab was hidden.

### Switch to terminal mode

By default, the extension opens a graphical chat panel. If you prefer the CLI-style interface, open the [Use Terminal setting](vscode://settings/claudeCode.useTerminal) and check the box.

You can also open VS Code settings (`Cmd+,` on Mac or `Ctrl+,` on Windows/Linux), go to Extensions → Claude Code, and check **Use Terminal**.

## Manage plugins

The VS Code extension includes a graphical interface for installing and managing [plugins](/en/plugins). Type `/plugins` in the prompt box to open the **Manage plugins** interface.

### Install plugins

The plugin dialog shows two tabs: **Plugins** and **Marketplaces**.

In the Plugins tab:

* **Installed plugins** appear at the top with toggle switches to enable or disable them
* **Available plugins** from your configured marketplaces appear below
* Search to filter plugins by name or description
* Click **Install** on any available plugin

When you install a plugin, choose the installation scope:

* **Install for you**: available in all your projects (user scope)
* **Install for this project**: shared with project collaborators (project scope)
* **Install locally**: only for you, only in this repository (local scope)

### Manage marketplaces

Switch to the **Marketplaces** tab to add or remove plugin sources:

* Enter a GitHub repo, URL, or local path to add a new marketplace
* Click the refresh icon to update a marketplace's plugin list
* Click the trash icon to remove a marketplace

After making changes, a banner prompts you to restart Claude Code to apply the updates.

<Note>
  Plugin management in VS Code uses the same CLI commands under the hood. Plugins and marketplaces you configure in the extension are also available in the CLI, and vice versa.
</Note>

For more about the plugin system, see [Plugins](/en/plugins) and [Plugin marketplaces](/en/plugin-marketplaces).

## Automate browser tasks with Chrome

Connect Claude to your Chrome browser to test web apps, debug with console logs, and automate browser workflows without leaving VS Code. This requires the [Claude in Chrome extension](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/claude/fcoeoabgfenejglbffodgkkbkcdhcgfn) version 1.0.36 or higher.

Type `@browser` in the prompt box followed by what you want Claude to do:

```text theme={null}
@browser go to localhost:3000 and check the console for errors
```

You can also open the attachment menu to select specific browser tools like opening a new tab or reading page content.

Claude opens new tabs for browser tasks and shares your browser's login state, so it can access any site you're already signed into.

For setup instructions, the full list of capabilities, and troubleshooting, see [Use Claude Code with Chrome](/en/chrome).

## VS Code commands and shortcuts

Open the Command Palette (`Cmd+Shift+P` on Mac or `Ctrl+Shift+P` on Windows/Linux) and type "Claude Code" to see all available VS Code commands for the Claude Code extension.

Some shortcuts depend on which panel is "focused" (receiving keyboard input). When your cursor is in a code file, the editor is focused. When your cursor is in Claude's prompt box, Claude is focused. Use `Cmd+Esc` / `Ctrl+Esc` to toggle between them.

<Note>
  These are VS Code commands for controlling the extension. Not all built-in Claude Code commands are available in the extension. See [VS Code extension vs. Claude Code CLI](#vs-code-extension-vs-claude-code-cli) for details.
</Note>

| Command                    | Shortcut                                                 | Description                                                                                               |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Focus Input                | `Cmd+Esc` (Mac) / `Ctrl+Esc` (Windows/Linux)             | Toggle focus between editor and Claude                                                                    |
| Open in Side Bar           | -                                                        | Open Claude in the left sidebar                                                                           |
| Open in Terminal           | -                                                        | Open Claude in terminal mode                                                                              |
| Open in New Tab            | `Cmd+Shift+Esc` (Mac) / `Ctrl+Shift+Esc` (Windows/Linux) | Open a new conversation as an editor tab                                                                  |
| Open in New Window         | -                                                        | Open a new conversation in a separate window                                                              |
| New Conversation           | `Cmd+N` (Mac) / `Ctrl+N` (Windows/Linux)                 | Start a new conversation. Requires Claude to be focused and `enableNewConversationShortcut` set to `true` |
| Insert @-Mention Reference | `Option+K` (Mac) / `Alt+K` (Windows/Linux)               | Insert a reference to the current file and selection (requires editor to be focused)                      |
| Show Logs                  | -                                                        | View extension debug logs                                                                                 |
| Logout                     | -                                                        | Sign out of your Anthropic account                                                                        |

### Launch a VS Code tab from other tools

The extension registers a URI handler at `vscode://anthropic.claude-code/open`. Use it to open a new Claude Code tab from your own tooling: a shell alias, a browser bookmarklet, or any script that can open a URL. If VS Code isn't already running, opening the URL launches it first. If VS Code is already running, the URL opens in whichever window is currently focused.

Invoke the handler with your operating system's URL opener. On macOS:

```bash theme={null}
open "vscode://anthropic.claude-code/open"
```

Use `xdg-open` on Linux or `start` on Windows.

The handler accepts two optional query parameters:

| Parameter | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `prompt`  | Text to pre-fill in the prompt box. Must be URL-encoded. The prompt is pre-filled but not submitted automatically.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `session` | A session ID to resume instead of starting a new conversation. The session must belong to the workspace currently open in VS Code. If the session isn't found, a fresh conversation starts instead. If the session is already open in a tab, that tab is focused. To capture a session ID programmatically, see [Continue conversations](/en/headless#continue-conversations). |

For example, to open a tab pre-filled with "review my changes":

```text theme={null}
vscode://anthropic.claude-code/open?prompt=review%20my%20changes
```

## Configure settings

The extension has two types of settings:

* **Extension settings** in VS Code: control the extension's behavior within VS Code. Open with `Cmd+,` (Mac) or `Ctrl+,` (Windows/Linux), then go to Extensions → Claude Code. You can also type `/` and select **General Config** to open settings.
* **Claude Code settings** in `~/.claude/settings.json`: shared between the extension and CLI. Use for allowed commands, environment variables, hooks, and MCP servers. See [Settings](/en/settings) for details.

<Tip>
  Add `"$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json"` to your `settings.json` to get autocomplete and inline validation for all available settings directly in VS Code.
</Tip>

### Extension settings

| Setting                           | Default   | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| --------------------------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `useTerminal`                     | `false`   | Launch Claude in terminal mode instead of graphical panel                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `initialPermissionMode`           | `default` | Controls approval prompts for new conversations: `default`, `plan`, `acceptEdits`, or `bypassPermissions`. See [permission modes](/en/permission-modes).                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `preferredLocation`               | `panel`   | Where Claude opens: `sidebar` (right) or `panel` (new tab)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `autosave`                        | `true`    | Auto-save files before Claude reads or writes them                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `useCtrlEnterToSend`              | `false`   | Use Ctrl/Cmd+Enter instead of Enter to send prompts                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `enableNewConversationShortcut`   | `false`   | Enable Cmd/Ctrl+N to start a new conversation                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `hideOnboarding`                  | `false`   | Hide the onboarding checklist (graduation cap icon)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `respectGitIgnore`                | `true`    | Exclude .gitignore patterns from file searches                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `usePythonEnvironment`            | `true`    | Activate the workspace's Python environment when running Claude. Requires the Python extension.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `environmentVariables`            | `[]`      | Set environment variables for the Claude process. Use Claude Code settings instead for shared config.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `disableLoginPrompt`              | `false`   | Skip authentication prompts (for third-party provider setups)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `allowDangerouslySkipPermissions` | `false`   | Adds [Auto mode](/en/permission-modes#eliminate-prompts-with-auto-mode) and Bypass permissions to the mode selector. Auto mode has [plan, admin, model, and provider requirements](/en/permission-modes#eliminate-prompts-with-auto-mode), so it may remain unavailable even with this toggle on. Use Bypass permissions only in sandboxes with no internet access. |
| `claudeProcessWrapper`            | -         | Executable path used to launch the Claude process                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

## VS Code extension vs. Claude Code CLI

Claude Code is available as both a VS Code extension (graphical panel) and a CLI (command-line interface in the terminal). Some features are only available in the CLI. If you need a CLI-only feature, run `claude` in VS Code's integrated terminal.

| Feature             | CLI                 | VS Code Extension                                                                    |
| ------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Commands and skills | [All](/en/commands) | Subset (type `/` to see available)                                                   |
| MCP server config   | Yes                 | Partial (add servers via CLI; manage existing servers with `/mcp` in the chat panel) |
| Checkpoints         | Yes                 | Yes                                                                                  |
| `!` bash shortcut   | Yes                 | No                                                                                   |
| Tab completion      | Yes                 | No                                                                                   |

### Rewind with checkpoints

The VS Code extension supports checkpoints, which track Claude's file edits and let you rewind to a previous state. Hover over any message to reveal the rewind button, then choose from three options:

* **Fork conversation from here**: start a new conversation branch from this message while keeping all code changes intact
* **Rewind code to here**: revert file changes back to this point in the conversation while keeping the full conversation history
* **Fork conversation and rewind code**: start a new conversation branch and revert file changes to this point

For full details on how checkpoints work and their limitations, see [Checkpointing](/en/checkpointing).

### Run CLI in VS Code

To use the CLI while staying in VS Code, open the integrated terminal (`` Ctrl+` `` on Windows/Linux or `` Cmd+` `` on Mac) and run `claude`. The CLI automatically integrates with your IDE for features like diff viewing and diagnostic sharing.

If using an external terminal, run `/ide` inside Claude Code to connect it to VS Code.

### Switch between extension and CLI

The extension and CLI share the same conversation history. To continue an extension conversation in the CLI, run `claude --resume` in the terminal. This opens an interactive picker where you can search for and select your conversation.

### Include terminal output in prompts

Reference terminal output in your prompts using `@terminal:name` where `name` is the terminal's title. This lets Claude see command output, error messages, or logs without copy-pasting.

### Monitor background processes

When Claude runs long-running commands, the extension shows progress in the status bar. However, visibility for background tasks is limited compared to the CLI. For better visibility, have Claude output the command so you can run it in VS Code's integrated terminal.

### Connect to external tools with MCP

MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers give Claude access to external tools, databases, and APIs.

To add an MCP server, open the integrated terminal (`` Ctrl+` `` or `` Cmd+` ``) and run `claude mcp add`. The example below adds GitHub's remote MCP server, which authenticates with a [personal access token](https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens) passed as a header:

```bash theme={null}
claude mcp add --transport http github https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/ \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_GITHUB_PAT"
```

Once configured, ask Claude to use the tools (e.g., "Review PR #456").

To manage MCP servers without leaving VS Code, type `/mcp` in the chat panel. The MCP management dialog lets you enable or disable servers, reconnect to a server, and manage OAuth authentication. See the [MCP documentation](/en/mcp) for available servers.

## Work with git

Claude Code integrates with git to help with version control workflows directly in VS Code. Ask Claude to commit changes, create pull requests, or work across branches.

### Create commits and pull requests

Claude can stage changes, write commit messages, and create pull requests based on your work:

```text theme={null}
> commit my changes with a descriptive message
> create a pr for this feature
> summarize the changes I've made to the auth module
```

When creating pull requests, Claude generates descriptions based on the actual code changes and can add context about testing or implementation decisions.

### Use git worktrees for parallel tasks

Use the `--worktree` (`-w`) flag to start Claude in an isolated worktree with its own files and branch:

```bash theme={null}
claude --worktree feature-auth
```

Each worktree maintains independent file state while sharing git history. This prevents Claude instances from interfering with each other when working on different tasks. For more details, see [Run parallel sessions with Git worktrees](/en/common-workflows#run-parallel-claude-code-sessions-with-git-worktrees).

## Use third-party providers

By default, Claude Code connects directly to Anthropic's API. If your organization uses Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, or Microsoft Foundry to access Claude, configure the extension to use your provider instead:

<Steps>
  <Step title="Disable login prompt">
    Open the [Disable Login Prompt setting](vscode://settings/claudeCode.disableLoginPrompt) and check the box.

    You can also open VS Code settings (`Cmd+,` on Mac or `Ctrl+,` on Windows/Linux), search for "Claude Code login", and check **Disable Login Prompt**.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Configure your provider">
    Follow the setup guide for your provider:

    * [Claude Code on Amazon Bedrock](/en/amazon-bedrock)
    * [Claude Code on Google Vertex AI](/en/google-vertex-ai)
    * [Claude Code on Microsoft Foundry](/en/microsoft-foundry)

    These guides cover configuring your provider in `~/.claude/settings.json`, which ensures your settings are shared between the VS Code extension and the CLI.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Security and privacy

Your code stays private. Claude Code processes your code to provide assistance but does not use it to train models. For details on data handling and how to opt out of logging, see [Data and privacy](/en/data-usage).

With auto-edit permissions enabled, Claude Code can modify VS Code configuration files (like `settings.json` or `tasks.json`) that VS Code may execute automatically. To reduce risk when working with untrusted code:

* Enable [VS Code Restricted Mode](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/workspace-trust#_restricted-mode) for untrusted workspaces
* Use manual approval mode instead of auto-accept for edits
* Review changes carefully before accepting them

### The built-in IDE MCP server

When the extension is active, it runs a local MCP server that the CLI connects to automatically. This is how the CLI opens diffs in VS Code's native diff viewer, reads your current selection for `@`-mentions, and — when you're working in a Jupyter notebook — asks VS Code to execute cells.

The server is named `ide` and is hidden from `/mcp` because there's nothing to configure. If your organization uses a `PreToolUse` hook to allowlist MCP tools, though, you'll need to know it exists.

**Transport and authentication.** The server binds to `127.0.0.1` on a random high port and is not reachable from other machines. Each extension activation generates a fresh random auth token that the CLI must present to connect. The token is written to a lock file under `~/.claude/ide/` with `0600` permissions in a `0700` directory, so only the user running VS Code can read it.

**Tools exposed to the model.** The server hosts a dozen tools, but only two are visible to the model. The rest are internal RPC the CLI uses for its own UI — opening diffs, reading selections, saving files — and are filtered out before the tool list reaches Claude.

| Tool name (as seen by hooks) | What it does                                                                                                              | Writes? |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| `mcp__ide__getDiagnostics`   | Returns language-server diagnostics — the errors and warnings in VS Code's Problems panel. Optionally scoped to one file. | No      |
| `mcp__ide__executeCode`      | Runs Python code in the active Jupyter notebook's kernel. See confirmation flow below.                                    | Yes     |

**Jupyter execution always asks first.** `mcp__ide__executeCode` can't run anything silently. On each call, the code is inserted as a new cell at the end of the active notebook, VS Code scrolls it into view, and a native Quick Pick asks you to **Execute** or **Cancel**. Cancelling — or dismissing the picker with `Esc` — returns an error to Claude and nothing runs. The tool also refuses outright when there's no active notebook, when the Jupyter extension (`ms-toolsai.jupyter`) isn't installed, or when the kernel isn't Python.

<Note>
  The Quick Pick confirmation is separate from `PreToolUse` hooks. An allowlist entry for `mcp__ide__executeCode` lets Claude *propose* running a cell; the Quick Pick inside VS Code is what lets it *actually* run.
</Note>

<a id="troubleshooting" />

## Fix common issues

### Extension won't install

* Ensure you have a compatible version of VS Code (1.98.0 or later)
* Check that VS Code has permission to install extensions
* Try installing directly from the [VS Code Marketplace](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=anthropic.claude-code)

### Spark icon not visible

The Spark icon appears in the **Editor Toolbar** (top-right of editor) when you have a file open. If you don't see it:

1. **Open a file**: The icon requires a file to be open. Having just a folder open isn't enough.
2. **Check VS Code version**: Requires 1.98.0 or higher (Help → About)
3. **Restart VS Code**: Run "Developer: Reload Window" from the Command Palette
4. **Disable conflicting extensions**: Temporarily disable other AI extensions (Cline, Continue, etc.)
5. **Check workspace trust**: The extension doesn't work in Restricted Mode

Alternatively, click "✱ Claude Code" in the **Status Bar** (bottom-right corner). This works even without a file open. You can also use the **Command Palette** (`Cmd+Shift+P` / `Ctrl+Shift+P`) and type "Claude Code".

### Claude Code never responds

If Claude Code isn't responding to your prompts:

1. **Check your internet connection**: Ensure you have a stable internet connection
2. **Start a new conversation**: Try starting a fresh conversation to see if the issue persists
3. **Try the CLI**: Run `claude` from the terminal to see if you get more detailed error messages

If problems persist, [file an issue on GitHub](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues) with details about the error.

## Uninstall the extension

To uninstall the Claude Code extension:

1. Open the Extensions view (`Cmd+Shift+X` on Mac or `Ctrl+Shift+X` on Windows/Linux)
2. Search for "Claude Code"
3. Click **Uninstall**

To also remove extension data and reset all settings:

```bash theme={null}
rm -rf ~/.vscode/globalStorage/anthropic.claude-code
```

For additional help, see the [troubleshooting guide](/en/troubleshooting).

## Next steps

Now that you have Claude Code set up in VS Code:

* [Explore common workflows](/en/common-workflows) to get the most out of Claude Code
* [Set up MCP servers](/en/mcp) to extend Claude's capabilities with external tools. Add servers using the CLI, then manage them with `/mcp` in the chat panel.
* [Configure Claude Code settings](/en/settings) to customize allowed commands, hooks, and more. These settings are shared between the extension and CLI.

## Adding MCP Servers: Claude Code CLI vs VS Code

Here's how to add MCP servers in each environment:

### 1. Claude Code CLI

**Three transport options:**

```bash
# HTTP (recommended for remote servers)
claude mcp add --transport http notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp

# SSE (deprecated but available)
claude mcp add --transport sse asana https://mcp.asana.com/sse

# Stdio (local processes)
claude mcp add --transport stdio airtable --env AIRTABLE_API_KEY=YOUR_KEY \
  -- npx -y airtable-mcp-server
```

**Three scope options:**

```bash
# Local scope (default) — private to you, this project only
claude mcp add --transport http stripe https://mcp.stripe.com

# Project scope — shared via .mcp.json in version control
claude mcp add --transport http paypal --scope project https://mcp.paypal.com/mcp

# User scope — available across all your projects
claude mcp add --transport http hubspot --scope user https://mcp.hubspot.com
```

**Manage servers:**

```bash
claude mcp list                # List all configured servers
claude mcp get github          # View details for a server
claude mcp remove github       # Remove a server
claude mcp reset-project-choices  # Reset approvals for project-scoped servers
```

**Key details:**

- Options (`--transport`, `--env`, `--scope`, `--header`) come **before** the server name
- `--` separates options from the server command (stdio only)
- Scopes store configs in:
  - `local`: `~/.claude.json` (project-specific, private)
  - `project`: `.mcp.json` at project root (shared with team)
  - `user`: `~/.claude.json` (all projects, private)

### 2. VS Code Integration

**Within VS Code, you have two paths:**

**Path A: CLI in integrated terminal**

Open the integrated terminal (`` Ctrl+` `` / `` Cmd+` ``) and run the same `claude mcp add` commands above. Servers added via CLI are immediately available in the extension.

**Path B: Manage servers via `/mcp` in chat**

Once servers are configured (via CLI), you can manage them directly in the VS Code chat:

- Type `/mcp` in the prompt box → opens MCP management dialog
- Enable/disable servers
- Reconnect to a server
- Manage OAuth authentication

**How inheritance works:**

The VS Code extension and CLI share the same configuration files:
- Both read from `~/.claude/settings.json` (settings layer)
- Both read from `.mcp.json` (project scope)
- MCP servers configured in the CLI are **automatically available** in the extension (no separate VS Code configuration needed)

---

## Practical Example

Add a GitHub MCP server for code reviews:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http github https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/ \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_GITHUB_PAT" --scope project
```

This creates `.mcp.json` in your project root. Both CLI and VS Code extension now have access. In VS Code, type `/mcp` to toggle it on or manage authentication.

- [VS Code extension guide](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/vs-code.md) (search for "Connect to external tools with MCP")

## Adding MCP servers

### In Claude Code (CLI and VS Code extension share the same config)

The CLI is the primary way — the VS Code extension inherits whatever you configure there.

**Add a server:**

```bash
# HTTP (most remote MCP servers)
claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url>

# HTTP with auth header
claude mcp add --transport http github https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/ \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_PAT"

# Stdio (local process)
claude mcp add --transport stdio airtable --env AIRTABLE_API_KEY=xxx \
  -- npx -y airtable-mcp-server
```

**Pick a scope with `--scope`:**

| Scope | Where it's stored | Who sees it |
|---|---|---|
| `local` (default) | `~/.claude.json` | You, this project only |
| `project` | `.mcp.json` at repo root | Whole team (commit it) |
| `user` | `~/.claude.json` | You, all projects |

**Manage:**

```bash
claude mcp list             # show configured servers
claude mcp get <name>       # details
claude mcp remove <name>    # remove
```

Inside Claude Code (CLI or VS Code extension), type `/mcp` to enable/disable servers, reconnect, or handle OAuth.

### In VS Code's native (non-Claude) MCP support

VS Code 1.102+ has its own MCP client separate from Claude Code. Configure it in a workspace or user `mcp.json`:

```jsonc
// .vscode/mcp.json  (or user settings)
{
  "servers": {
    "github": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${env:GITHUB_PAT}" }
    }
  }
}
```

This is consumed by GitHub Copilot's agent mode in VS Code — it is **not** the same registry the Claude Code extension uses. So if you want a server in both, you configure it in both places.

### Quick rule of thumb

- Using the Claude Code VS Code extension → add via `claude mcp add ...` in a terminal. Nothing else needed.
- Using Copilot agent mode in VS Code → add via `.vscode/mcp.json`.
- Want it shared with teammates → use `--scope project` (Claude Code) or commit `.vscode/mcp.json` (VS Code native).

Docs: [Claude Code MCP](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md), [Claude Code VS Code extension](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/vs-code.md).

The board features a 22-pin FPC/FFC connector (J29) with 0.5 mm pitch, similar to the one used for the Raspberry Pi Compute Module boards. 4-lane MIPI cameras can connect to the board directly, while 2-lane cameras and displays provided by Raspberry Pi^[(1)](GUID-C898D0DE-85AB-4956-9D37-ECB937CDC470.html#GUID-C898D0DE-85AB-4956-9D37-ECB937CDC470__GUID-A76F9D3F-E9D8-4497-8B37-27260EE18064)^ require a 22-pin to 15-pin FPC adapter. For 4-lane MIPI displays, an adapter is necessary due to various non-standard connector pinout across different manufacturers. Additional GPIOs and TWI interface are provided for camera/display control. Note: 1. Raspberry Pi is a trademark of Raspberry Pi Trading. The following figure shows the MIPI CSI camera interface. The following table shows the MIPI CSI/DSI interface signal description. | Pin No. | PIO | Signal Name | Signal Description | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19 | \u2013 | GND | Ground | | 2 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_D0\\_N | MIPI D-PHY negative differential input data 0 | | 3 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_D0\\_P | MIPI D-PHY positive differential input data 0 | | 5 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_D1\\_N | MIPI D-PHY negative differential input data 1 | | 6 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_D1\\_P | MIPI D-PHY positive differential input data 1 | | 8 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_CK\\_N | MIPI D-PHY negative differential input clock | | 9 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_CK\\_P | MIPI D-PHY positive differential input clock | | 11 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_D2\\_N | MIPI D-PHY negative differential input data 2 | | 12 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_D2\\_P | MIPI D-PHY positive differential input data 2 | | 14 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_D3\\_N | MIPI D-PHY negative differential input data 3 | | 15 | \u2013 | MIPI\\_D3\\_P | MIPI D-PHY positive differential input data 3 | | 17 | PC19 | MIPI\\_CSI\\_GPIO0 | General Purpose I/O | | 18 | PC15 | MIPI\\_CSI\\_GPIO1 | General Purpose I/O | | 20 | PA25 | CAM\\_I\u00B2C\\_CLK\\_ | TWI Clock | | 21 | PA24 | CAM\\_I\u00B2C\\_DATA | TWI Data | | 22 | \u2013 | VDD\\_3V3 or 5V\\_MAIN | 3.3V or 5V |\\n\\n Images: https://onlinedocs.microchip.com/oxy/GUID-69CFF0CC-BD83-4DB3-AA72-E309A819F68E-en-US-3/GUID-C363CF13-ABF3-4ECC-A292-836C41C8662A-high.png","url":"https://onlinedocs.microchip.com/oxy/GUID-69CFF0CC-BD83-4DB3-AA72-E309A819F68E-en-US-3/GUID-C898D0DE-85AB-4956-9D37-ECB937CDC470.html?utm_source=mchpmcp","keywords":["3.4.10 MIPI CSI/DSI Interface - SAM9X75-Curiosity","SAM9X75-Curiosity"],"relevancyScore":125.306595},{"title":"SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board - Features","content":"{{OnThisPage depth=\u00223\u0022/}}\n\nThis topic describes the features of the [SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board (P/N: EV31H43A)](https://www.microchip.com/en-us/development-tool/EV31H43A) with links to additional information.\n\n## Features Summary\nThe major features of the SAM9X60-EK Evaluation Kit are:\n\n- SAM9X75D2G MPU\n- Mass storage\n- Communications\n- Debugging\n- User interface\n- Expansion\n- Power options\n- Jumper summary\n\n### References\n- [SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/software-tools/mcu-dev-boards/32-bit-kits/sam9x75-ev-curiosity/introduction/WebHome)\n\n[SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/image:sam9x75d2g/png)\n\n## SAM9X75D2G MPU\nThe [SAM9X75D2G](https://www.microchip.com/en-us/product/SAM9X75D2G) System-in-Package (SiP) is a high-performance, ultra-low-power ARM926EJ-S\u2122 Arm\u003Csup\u003E\u00AE\u003C/sup\u003E Thumb\u003Csup\u003E\u00AE\u003C/sup\u003E CPU-based embedded microprocessor (MPU) running up to 800 MHz, with a 2 Gbit integrated DDR3L memory. Its features include:\n\n- 800 MHz ARM926EJ-S Core, 266 MHz System/Memory Bus\n- 2 Gbit integrated DDR3L Memory\n- 64 kB internal SRAM\n- MIPI Display Serial Interface (MIPI DSI\u003Csup\u003E\u00AE\u003C/sup\u003E) and LVDS display interface\n- 2D graphics processor unit\n- MIPI-CSI-2 Camera interface\n- A Gigabit Ethernet interface through SODIMM 260-pin connector\n- Dual Control Area Network (CAN)\n- One microSD card interface, One M.2 Key E connector/radio module interface\n- One Micro-B USB device, two USB Type-A connectors\n- Thirteen FLEXCOMs (Universal Synchronous Asynchronous Receiver Transmitter (USART), Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI), and Inter-Integrated Circuit (I2C))\n- Hardware encryption engine and True Random Number Generator (TRNG)\n- Secure boot\n\n## Mass Storage\nThere are three mass storage options available on the development board.\n\n### 4 Gb NAND Flash (U5)\nU3 is a 4 Gb (512M x 8) NAND Flash memory ([Macronix](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/url:https://www/macronix/com/en-us/Pages/default/aspx) MX30LF4G28AD-XKI). It is connected to the NAND Flash controller of the SAM9X75D2G.\n\n### 64 Mb Serial Quad I/O (SQI) Flash Device with EUI-48 and EUI-64 (U6)\nU6 is a 64 Mb Serial Quad I/O\u2122 (SQI\u2122) flash device with EUI-48 and EUI-64 memory ([Microchip SST26VF064BEUI](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/url:https://www/microchip/com/en-us/product/sst26vf064beui)). It is connected to the Quad SPI Interface peripheral of the SAM9x75D2G.\n\n### Micro Secure Digital (J14)\nJ14 is a microSD memory card slot. It is connected to the Secure Digital MultiMediaCard port 0 (SDMMC0) peripheral of the SAM9X75D2G.\n\n![sam9x75 Curiosity Mass Storage](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/download/attachments/sam9x75_massstorage.png)\n\n## Communications\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board provides wired communications via Ethernet, USB, and CAN.\n\n![sam9x75 Curiosity Mass Storage](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/download/attachments/peripherals.png)\n\n### Ethernet (J17)\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board features a Gigabit Ethernet interface through a SODIMM 260-pin connector. The SAM9X75 Curiosity LAN kit comes with a [LAN8840 EDS2 daughter card](https://www.microchip.com/en-us/development-tool/ev12n54a) to evaluate the Microchip LAN8840 Gigabit Ethernet RGMII Ethernet PHYOne Gigabit Ethernet interface through the SODIMM 260-pin connector.\n\n### CAN Interface\nThe SAM9X75-Curiosity board shares the CAN interface with the UART signals of the mikroBUS\u2122 connector (J25). Use the mikroBUS Click MIKROE-2299 that embeds a Microchip MCP2542WFD to connect the SAM9X75 Curiosity to a CAN.\n\n### USB (J2, J15 and J16)\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board features three USB communication ports (J2 - USB 2.0 Micro-B (USB-A), J15 - USB Type-A (USB-B), J16 - USB Type-A (USB-C)).\n\nThe USB-A port acts only as a USB device interface and is accessed via USB Micro-B connector J7.\n\n\u003E Note: The USB-A port (J2) is used as a power source for the development board.\n\n\u003E Note: The USB-A port (J2) is used as the default serial port used to communicate with the [SAM-BA\u003Csup\u003E\u00AE\u003C/sup\u003E monitor](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/software-tools/programmers-and-debuggers/32-bit-isp/monitor/WebHome) resident on the MPU.\n\nThe USB-B and USB-C ports are connected to the stacked USB Type-A connecter (J15 \u0026 J16). Each port can act both as a device and as a host.\n\n### Wireless M.2 interface (J20)\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity board embeds an M.2 connector to interconnect with wireless modules. M.2 (formerly known as NGFF) is a small form factor card and connector that supports applications such as Wi-Fi\u003Csup\u003E\u00AE\u003C/sup\u003E, WLAN, USB, PCIe\u003Csup\u003E\u00AE\u003C/sup\u003E and SATA, as defined in the PCI-SIG\u003Csup\u003E\u00AE\u003C/sup\u003E M.2 Specification. The default interface used with the wireless module solution is the SDIO. However, the wireless module can be controlled in SPI mode and configuration can be performed manually by the end user. The interface is based on a 67-pin connector and includes a clock, SDIO/SPI interface, USART Interface, wake-up/interrupt, reset, and power lines.\n\n## Debugging\nThere is one method of debugging the SAM9X75 Curiosity Development board via JTAG. In addition, a console serial communication port (J11) is available for debugging.\n\n### JTAG (J34)\nA JTAG interface to the SAM9X75-Curiosity is provided by 20-pin connector J34. This facilitates software development and debugging by connecting an external JTAG debugger such as the [MPLAB\u00AE PICkit\u2122 5 In-Circuit Debugger](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/url:https://www/microchip/com/en-us/development-tool/pg164150) or [J-32 Debug Probe](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/url:https://www/microchip/com/en-us/development-tool/DV164232).\n\n\u003E Alert: The JTAG interface signals voltage levels are 3.3V.\n\n### Serial UART Debug Port (J35)\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board features a dedicated serial UART port (J35) (3.3 VDC TTL level) for communicating with the target console.\n\n{{info}}\nNote: For more information, see the \u0022//[SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board - Console Serial Communications](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/software-tools/mcu-dev-boards/32-bit-kits/sam9x75-ev-curiosity/console-serial-communications/WebHome)//\u0022 page.\n{{/info}}\n\n## User Interface\n### Red-Green-Blue (RGB) LED (LD1)\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board features one RGB LED (LD1).\n\n### Pushbuttons (SW1-SW4)\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board contains four push buttons:\n\n- USER (SW1): User push button which is available for user\u2019s usage\n- WKUP (SW2): Will wake up the processor when it has been shut down by software\n- RESET (SW3): Reset push button, when pressed the system resets\n- START (SW4): When pressed, the PMIC start-up sequence is initiated if the buck converters are off\n\n### LCD Interface (J28, J29)\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board contains both LVDS display interface(J28) and MIPI display serial interface(J29).\n\nCompatible Microchip LCD modules (LVDS Display [AC69T88A](https://www.microchip.com/en-us/development-tool/AC69T88A)  and MIPI DSI [AC40T08A](https://www.microchip.com/en-us/development-tool/ac40t08a) ) can be connected to the SAM9X75 Curiosity board.\n\n### MIPI CSI/DSI (J29)\nThe SAM9X75-Curiosity board embeds a 4-lane MIPI D-PHY for interfacing with CSI-compatible cameras and DSI-compatible displays.\n\n## Expansion\n### mikroBUS\u2122 (25)\nThe [mikroBUS](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/url:https://www/mikroe/com/mikrobus) socket is a proprietary communication and plugin standard for small interface boards called [Click boards\u2122](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/url:https://www/mikroe/com/click) that extends the capabilities of the development board by offering SPI, UART, TWI, and PWM-based sensors and devices. They are made by [MikroElektronika](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/url:https://www/mikroe/com/click), a producer and retailer of hardware and software tools for developing embedded systems.\n\n### GPIO/Raspberry Pi Connector(J27)\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board contains a 40-pin GPIO connector (J27) for use. This connector is compatible with the Raspberry Pi expansion header.\n\n## Power Options\nTwo options are available to power up the SAM9X75-Curiosity board, powering through the jack connector (J1) or powering through the USB Micro-B connector on the USBA port (J2).\n\n## Jumper Summary\nThe SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board has 9 jumpers. Refer to Section 2.5 of the \u0022//[SAM9X75 Curiosity User Guide](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/aemDocuments/documents/MPU32/ProductDocuments/UserGuides/SAM9X75-Curiosity-User-Guide-DS60001859.pdf)//\u0022 for default jumper settings.\n\n## Learn More\n- [SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board \u2013 Introduction](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/software-tools/mcu-dev-boards/32-bit-kits/sam9x75-ev-curiosity/introduction/WebHome)\n- [SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board \u2013 Console Serial Port](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/software-tools/mcu-dev-boards/32-bit-kits/sam9x75-ev-curiosity/console-serial-communications/WebHome)\n- [SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board \u2013 Booting Demo Linux\u003Csup\u003E\u00AE\u003C/sup\u003E Image](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/software-tools/mcu-dev-boards/32-bit-kits/sam9x75-ev-curiosity/booting-demo-linux-image/WebHome)\n- [Developing with Embedded Linux](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/software-tools/linux/WebHome)\n- [Developing Applications with MPLAB Harmony 3 Software Framework for MPUs](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/software-tools/32-bit-harmony-v3/WebHome)","url":"https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/software-tools/mcu-dev-boards/32-bit-kits/sam9x75-ev-curiosity/features/?utm_source=mchpmcp","keywords":["SAM9X75 Curiosity Development Board - The SAM9X75-Curiosity board delivers the needed performance, from power management and timing to storage and communication interfacing. SAM9X75-Curiosity follows the Microchip MPU strategy for versatile evaluation kits, showcasing all the features that the SAM9X75D2G MPU can offer. This differentiated offering allows designers to immediately focus on delivering their design.","url":"https://onlinedocs.microchip.com/oxy/GUID-69CFF0CC-BD83-4DB3-AA72-E309A819F68E-en-US-3/GUID-B5DA63AD-255C-4538-8499-C8ED5F2EA8A2.html?utm_source=mchpmcp","keywords":["2 Product Overview - SAM9X75-Curiosity","SAM9X75-Curiosity"],"relevancyScore":74.26979},{"title":"4.2 Board Setup - SAM9X75-Curiosity","content":"# 4.2 Board Setup Follow these steps before using the SAM9X75-Curiosity board: 1. Unpack the board, taking care to avoid electrostatic discharge. 2. Check the default jumper settings (see [Default Jumper Settings](GUID-1DA275D3-3C64-403A-A95B-1F054B039241.html)). 3. Connect the Micro-USB cable to connector J2 (USB-A port). 4. Connect the other end of the cable to a free port on your PC. 5. Connect a USB-UART converter to J35, making sure to also connect the VBUS\\_FTDI power source. 6. Open a terminal (console 115200, N, 8, 1) on your PC for the USB-UART converter. 7. Reset the board. A \u201CROMCode\u201D startup message appears on the console.","url":"https://onlinedocs.microchip.com/oxy/GUID-69CFF0CC-BD83-4DB3-AA72-E309A819F68E-en-US-3/GUID-25BB5ED1-A447-4456-B0C1-E2A7166E31DF.html?utm_source=mchpmcp","keywords":["4.2 Board Setup - SAM9X75-Curiosity","SAM9X75-Curiosity"],"relevancyScore":84.67282},{"title":"3.2.6 Standard Serial Communication Interfaces Distribution - SAM9X75-Curiosity","content":"# 3.2.6 Standard Serial Communication Interfaces Distribution SAM9X75-Curiosity features several devices and interfaces that use UART, SPI and TWI interfaces. Got a definitive answer from the Microchip MCP. The J29 22-pin connector pinout on the Curiosity (from §3.4.10 of the user guide) is:

| Pin | PIO | Signal |
|---|---|---|
| 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19 | — | GND |
| 2 / 3 | — | MIPI_D0_N / MIPI_D0_P |
| **5 / 6** | — | **MIPI_D1_N / MIPI_D1_P** |
| 8 / 9 | — | MIPI_CK_N / MIPI_CK_P |
| 11 / 12 | — | MIPI_D2_N / MIPI_D2_P |
| 14 / 15 | — | MIPI_D3_N / MIPI_D3_P |
| **17** | **PC19** | **MIPI_CSI_GPIO0** |
| **18** | **PC15** | **MIPI_CSI_GPIO1** |
| 20 | PA25 | CAM_I²C_CLK |
| 21 | PA24 | CAM_I²C_DATA |
| 22 | — | VDD_3V3 or 5V_MAIN |

So your mapping was off by one or two rows in the datasheet — **PC19 is on pin 17 (not 6), and PC15 is on pin 18 (not 5)**. Pins 5 and 6 are MIPI_D1_N/P, which are CSI data lane 1 differential signals — not driven by GPIOs at all. The good news is that PC19/PC15 are in fact dedicated GPIOs on the camera connector (labeled `MIPI_CSI_GPIO0/1`), so they're the right pins to use for RESET/INT — we just need the 22→15 adapter to carry pins 17 and 18 through, and the Waveshare board to expose its TC358743 RESET on the matching 15-pin side.

Also confirmed from the same table: the FLEXCOM6 TWI we were planning to use is **not** the right I2C bus. The camera connector's I2C is `CAM_I²C_CLK = PA25` and `CAM_I²C_DATA = PA24`, shared with the M.2/PMIC/LVDS bus. That I2C goes through a different FLEXCOM instance — I need to verify which one marvin's MCC config points at.

Confirmation on the I2C — FLEXCOM6 on PA24/PA25 **is** on the camera connector's I2C lines per [pin_configurations.csv:85-86](firmware/marvin/default/src/config/default/pin_configurations.csv#L85-L86). So I2C path is fine; I retract what I said about it being the wrong bus.

So the corrected picture is:

| Marvin MCC name | SAM9X75 pin | J29 pin | Signal on J29 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `CAMERA_RESET` | PC19 | **17** | MIPI_CSI_GPIO0 |
| `CAMERA_PWD` | PC15 | **18** | MIPI_CSI_GPIO1 |
| I2C SDA | PA24 | 21 | CAM_I²C_DATA |
| I2C SCL | PA25 | 20 | CAM_I²C_CLK |

Good news: PC19/PC15 are dedicated GPIOs (`MIPI_CSI_GPIO0/1`) on the connector, so they're the right pins to use for RESET/INT.

**Real question now:** does your 22→15 pin adapter cable carry J29 pins 17 and 18 through to the 15-pin side, **and** does the Waveshare v1/v2 expose the TC358743 RESET_N on the 15-pin FFC? My recollection on the Waveshare HDMI-to-CSI boards is that they often have an on-board RC reset network and **don't** route the chip's RESET_N out to the 15-pin FFC — in which case we physically can't drive it from the SAM9X75.

This isn't a blocker: the TC358743 has a **software reset** (register `SYSCTL.Sreset` in the bridge section, plus `CONFCTL.SleepM`). The kernel driver uses it. If hardware RESET is unreachable, we just do software reset after power-up, and we're fine.

Let me update the journal with the corrected pinout and this finding.

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-01 14:20:23Z)**_

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-01 14:20:33Z)**_

Two questions in one — let me separate them.

### Is the connector numbering backwards from yours?

Yes, mathematically exactly reversed. If you flip pin numbering end-for-end:

| Your number | `22 + 1 − N` | Microchip's number | Signal |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | `22 − 5 + 1 = 18` | 18 | PC15 (MIPI_CSI_GPIO1) ✓ |
| 6 | `22 − 6 + 1 = 17` | 17 | PC19 (MIPI_CSI_GPIO0) ✓ |

So you were counting from the opposite end of the FFC. Easy mistake — FPC/FFC connectors number from a specific physical end, indicated by a silkscreen triangle or the "pin 1" marking on the connector housing, and which end is "pin 1" depends on the board side you're looking at.

Microchip's numbering (per User Guide §3.4.10) is the authoritative one for the J29 connector, and it matches the Raspberry Pi CM4 22-pin camera convention. Pin 1 is the GND immediately adjacent to MIPI_D0_N; pin 22 is the power pin (3V3 or 5V).

### Is the signal ordering itself unusual? (D0 / D1 / CK / D2 / D3)

No — this is the **standard CSI-2 FFC layout** used by every RPi camera/CM4 board and by most MIPI CSI-2 connectors that follow the RPi convention. The reason for this ordering (rather than e.g. CK / D0 / D1 / D2 / D3) is signal integrity:

- CSI-2 always uses lane 0 + clock; lanes 1–3 are optional.
- Putting the clock **in the middle** of the active data lanes minimizes the skew between clock and the farthest data lane. With D0/D1/CK/D2/D3, every data lane is within two pair-slots of the clock.
- In a 2-lane cable (D0 + D1 + CK) the clock ends up symmetrically between the two data pairs — which is also what the Waveshare v1/v2 15-pin adapter sees.

So the layout isn't "wrong", and it's not reversed at the signal-assignment level — it's deliberate. The numbering direction on the connector is the only thing that got flipped in our communication.

### Practical implication

None for our plan. I2C (pins 20/21 Microchip-numbered = pins 2/3 from the "wrong" end) is symmetric about center either way, and we've decided to use software reset via I2C for Phase 1. So the inverted read doesn't change anything — the journal already reflects the correct pinout.

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-01 14:22:59Z)**_

Acknowledged — schematic vs. pinout-table numbering inversions are frustrating and common. The schematic typically shows the mated connector as the device sees it, while the pinout table often shows the physical housing pin order. Signals don't care; cable orientation does, and you've confirmed that works.

Phase 0 is fully closed. Ready for Phase 1 whenever you want to pick it up.

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-01 14:25:46Z)**_

Got everything I need. DBGU is retargeted to `printf` via [xc32_monitor.c:62-69](firmware/marvin/default/src/config/default/stdio/xc32_monitor.c), and Harmony's I2C API is async callback-based (`DRV_I2C_WriteReadTransferAdd` does a write-then-repeated-start-read in one go — perfect for register reads). Also found the kernel driver's probe check at [tc358743.c:2210-2215](../linux-at91/drivers/media/i2c/tc358743.c#L2210-L2215): `(CHIPID & 0xff00) != 0` → rejected. So the pass condition is "upper byte of the 16-bit CHIPID register is zero", not a specific magic number.

Writing detailed Phase 1 to the journal now.

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-01 14:26:39Z)**_

Phase 1 plan is in the journal. Key points to review:

**Shape:**
- New module `default/src/tc358743.{c,h}`, flat under `src/` (throwaway-friendly per our Phase 3 deferral).
- Hooks in via `TC358743_Initialize()` in `APP_Initialize()` and `TC358743_Tasks()` at the top of `APP_Tasks()`.
- Uses Harmony's async I2C API (`DRV_I2C_Open` + `DRV_I2C_WriteReadTransferAdd` + transfer-event callback).
- `printf` goes out DBGU for free — no retargeting work.

**Runtime sequence:**
1. Open DRV_I2C_INDEX_0, register callback.
2. Software reset: write `0x0001` to `SYSCTL` (reg `0x0002`). Wire bytes: `0x00 0x02 0x01 0x00`.
3. Wait ≥1 ms.
4. Release reset: write `0x0000` to `SYSCTL`. Wire bytes: `0x00 0x02 0x00 0x00`.
5. Wait ≥1 ms.
6. Read `CHIPID` (reg `0x0000`, 2 bytes back). Wire: write `0x00 0x00`, then read 2 bytes.
7. Print the two bytes; pass if the high byte is `0x00` (matches kernel driver's [tc358743.c:2210-2215](../linux-at91/drivers/media/i2c/tc358743.c#L2210-L2215) probe check).

**Concrete open implementation choice when we pick this up:**

Delay mechanism for the two ≥1 ms waits. Options, in order of increasing effort:
- Busy-wait loop tuned to CPU frequency (crude but fine for Phase 1).
- Poll a SYSTICK counter if one's already running.
- Add a proper `TIME_` service.

I'll pick the simplest at implementation time unless you want to commit to one now.

Let me know when you're ready to proceed to implementation (or if anything in the plan needs adjusting).

553	
554	   Description:
555	        Creates a timer object and registers a function with it to be called back
556	        when the requested delay (specified in microseconds) has completed.  The
557	        caller must identify if the timer should call the function once or repeatedly
558	        every time the given delay period expires.
559	
560	   Precondition:
561	        The SYS_TIME_Initialize function should have been called before calling this
562	        function.
563	
564	   Parameters:
565	    callback    - Pointer to the function to be called.
566	                  For single shot timers, the callback cannot be NULL.
567	                  For periodic timers, if the callback pointer is given as NULL,
568	                  no callback will occur, but SYS_TIME_TimerPeriodHasExpired can
569	                  still be polled to determine if the period has expired for a
570	                  periodic timer.
571	
572	    context     - A client-defined value that is passed to the callback function.
573	
574	    us          - Time period in microseconds.
575	
576	    type        - Type of callback requested. If type is SYS_TIME_SINGLE, the
577	                  Callback function will be called once when the time period expires.
578	                  After the time period expires, the timer object will be freed.
579	                  If type is SYS_TIME_PERIODIC Callback function will be called
580	                  repeatedly, every time the time period expires until the timer
581	                  object is stopped or deleted.
582	
583	
584	   Returns:
585	        SYS_TIME_HANDLE - A valid timer object handle if the call succeeds.
586	                      SYS_TIME_HANDLE_INVALID if it fails.
587	
588	   Example:
589	      Given a callback function implementation matching the following prototype:
590	      <code>
591	      void MyCallback ( uintptr_t context);
592	      </code>
593	
594	      The following example call will register it, requesting a 500 microsecond
595	      periodic callback.
596	      <code>
597	     
598	      SYS_TIME_HANDLE handle = SYS_TIME_CallbackRegisterUS(MyCallback, (uintptr_t)0, 500, SYS_TIME_PERIODIC);
599	      if (handle != SYS_TIME_HANDLE_INVALID)
600	      {
601	           
602	      }
603	      </code>
604	
605	   Remarks:
606	       Will give a callback after the requested number of microseconds or longer
607	       have elapsed, depending on system performance. In tick-based mode, the requested
608	       delay will be ceiled to the next timer tick. For example, if the 
609	       timer tick is set to 1 msec and the requested delay is 1500 usec, a 
610	       delay of 2 msec will be generated.
611	
612	       Delay values of 0 will return SYS_TIME_ERROR.
613	*/
614	
615	SYS_TIME_HANDLE SYS_TIME_CallbackRegisterUS ( SYS_TIME_CALLBACK callback, uintptr_t context,
616	                                              uint32_t us, SYS_TIME_CALLBACK_TYPE type );
617	
618	
619	// *****************************************************************************
620	/* Function:
621	    SYS_TIME_HANDLE SYS_TIME_CallbackRegisterMS ( SYS_TIME_CALLBACK callback,
622	                        uintptr_t context, uint32_t ms, SYS_TIME_CALLBACK_TYPE type )
623	
624	   Summary:
625	        Registers a function with the time system service to be called back when the
626	        requested number of milliseconds has expired (either once or repeatedly).
627	
628	   Description:
629	        Creates a timer object and registers a function with it to be called back
630	        when the requested delay (specified in milliseconds) has completed.  The
631	        caller must identify if the timer should call the function once or repeatedly
632	        every time the given delay period expires.
633	
634	   Precondition:
635	        The SYS_TIME_Initialize function should have been called before calling this
636	        function.
637	
638	   Parameters:
639	        callback    - Pointer to the function to be called.
640	                      For single shot timers, the callback cannot be NULL.
641	                      For periodic timers, if the callback pointer is given as NULL,
642	                      no callback will occur, but SYS_TIME_TimerPeriodHasExpired can
643	                      still be polled to determine if the period has expired for a
644	                      periodic timer.
645	
646	        context     - A client-defined value that is passed to the callback function.
647	
648	        ms          - Time period in milliseconds.
649	
650	        type        - Type of callback requested. If type is SYS_TIME_SINGLE, the
651	                      Callback function will be called once when the time period expires.
652	                      After the time period expires, the timer object will be freed.
653	                      If type is SYS_TIME_PERIODIC Callback function will be called
654	                      repeatedly, every time the time period expires until the timer
655	                      object is stopped or deleted.
656	
657	
658	   Returns:
659	        SYS_TIME_HANDLE - A valid timer object handle if the call succeeds.
660	                          SYS_TIME_HANDLE_INVALID if it fails.
661	
662	   Example:
663	      Given a callback function implementation matching the following prototype:
664	      <code>
665	      void MyCallback ( uintptr_t context);
666	      </code>
667	
668	      The following example call will register it, requesting a 50 millisecond
669	      periodic callback.
670	      <code>
671	     
672	      SYS_TIME_HANDLE handle = SYS_TIME_CallbackRegisterMS(MyCallback, (uintptr_t)0, 50, SYS_TIME_PERIODIC);
673	      if (handle != SYS_TIME_HANDLE_INVALID)
674	      {
675	           
676	      }
677	      </code>
678	      
679	    Remarks:
680	       Will give a callback after the requested number of microseconds or longer
681	       have elapsed, depending on system performance. In tick-based mode, the requested
682	       delay will be ceiled to the next timer tick. For example, if the 
683	       timer tick is set to 700 usec and the requested delay is 2 msec, a delay
684	       of 2.1 ms will be generated.
685	
686	       Delay values of 0 will return SYS_TIME_ERROR.
687	*/
688	
689	SYS_TIME_HANDLE SYS_TIME_CallbackRegisterMS ( SYS_TIME_CALLBACK callback, uintptr_t context,
690	                                              uint32_t ms, SYS_TIME_CALLBACK_TYPE type );

700	/* Function:
701	    uint32_t SYS_TIME_FrequencyGet ( void )
702	
703	  Summary:
704	    Gets the frequency at which the hardwaer timer counts.
705	
706	  Description:
707	    For tick-less mode this API returns the frequency at which the hardware 
708	    timer runs. 
709	    For tick-based mode, this API returns the frequency at which the hardware
710	    timer generates a periodic tick.
711	    This frequency determines the maximum resolution of all 
712	    services provided by SYS_TIME.
713	
714	  Precondition:
715	    The SYS_TIME_Initialize function should have been called before calling this
716	    function.
717	
718	  Parameters:
719	    None
720	
721	  Returns:
722	    If the timer has been initialized and is ready:
723	    For tick-less mode this API returns the frequency at which the hardware 
724	    timer runs. 
725	    For tick-based mode, this API returns the frequency at which the hardware
726	    timer generates a periodic tick.
727	    Returns 0 if the timer is not initialized.
728	
729	  Example:
730	    <code>
731	    uint32_t frequency = SYS_TIME_FrequencyGet();
732	    </code>
733	
734	  Remarks:
735	    This frequency is determined by hardware capabilities and how they are
736	    configured and initialized.
737	*/
738	
739	uint32_t SYS_TIME_FrequencyGet ( void );
740	
741	
742	// *****************************************************************************
743	/* Function:
744	    uint32_t SYS_TIME_CounterGet ( void )
745	
746	  Summary:
747	    Get the common 32-bit system counter value.
748	
749	  Description:
750	    Returns the current "live" value of the common 32-bit system counter.
751	
752	  Precondition:
753	    The SYS_TIME_Initialize function should have been called before calling this
754	    function.
755	
756	  Parameters:
757	    None
758	
759	  Returns:
760	    The current "live" value of the common 32-bit system counter.
761	
762	  Example:
763	    <code>
764	    uint32_t timeStamp1;
765	    uint32_t timeStamp2;
766	    uint32_t timeDiffMs;
767	 
768	    timeStamp1 = SYS_TIME_CounterGet();
769	   
770	    timeStamp2 = SYS_TIME_CounterGet();    
771	
772	    timeDiffMs = SYS_TIME_CountToMS((timeStamp2 - timeStamp1));
773	    </code>
774	
775	  Remarks:
776	    The value returned may be stale as soon as it is provided, as the timer is
777	    live and running at full frequency resolution (as configured and as reported
778	    by the SYS_TIME_FrequencyGet function). If additional accuracy is required,
779	    use a hardware timer instance.
780	*/
781	
782	uint32_t SYS_TIME_CounterGet ( void );
783	
784	// *****************************************************************************
785	/* Function:
786	    uint64_t SYS_TIME_Counter64Get ( void )
787	
788	  Summary:
789	    Get the common 64-bit system counter value.
790	
791	  Description:
792	    Returns the current "live" value of the common 64-bit system counter.
793	
794	  Precondition:
795	    The SYS_TIME_Initialize function should have been called before calling this
796	    function.
797	
798	  Parameters:
799	    None
800	
801	  Returns:
802	    The current "live" value of the common 64-bit system counter.
803	
804	  Example:
805	    <code>
806	    uint64_t timeStamp1;
807	    uint64_t timeStamp2;
808	    uint64_t timeDiffMs;
809	  
810	    timeStamp1 = SYS_TIME_Counter64Get();
811	 
812	    timeStamp2 = SYS_TIME_Counter64Get();
813	  
814	    timeDiffMs = timeStamp2 - timeStamp1;
815	    timeDiffMs = (uint64_t)(((double)timeDiffMs/SYS_TIME_FrequencyGet())*1000.0);
816	    </code>
817	
818	  Remarks:
819	    The value returned may be stale as soon as it is provided, as the timer is
820	    live and running at full frequency resolution (as configured and as reported
821	    by the SYS_TIME_FrequencyGet function). If additional accuracy is required,
822	    use a hardware timer instance.
823	*/
824	
825	uint64_t SYS_TIME_Counter64Get ( void );
826

835	    Sets the current "live" value of the common 32-bit system counter.

838	    The SYS_TIME_Initialize function should have been called before calling this

857	// *****************************************************************************
858	/* Function:
859	      uint32_t SYS_TIME_CountToUS ( uint32_t count )
860	
861	   Summary:
862	      Converts a counter value to time interval in microseconds.
863	
864	   Description:
865	      This function converts a counter value to time interval in
866	      microseconds, based on the hardware timer frequency as configured
867	      and as reported by SYS_TIME_FrequencyGet.
868	
869	   Precondition:
870	      The SYS_TIME_Initialize function should have been called before calling
871	      this function.
872	
873	   Parameters:
874	      count  - Counter value to be converted to an equivalent value in
875	               microseconds.
876	
877	   Returns:
878	      Number of microseconds represented by the given counter value.
879	
880	   Example:
881	      Given a previously captured 32-bit counter value called "timestamp"
882	      captured using the SYS_TIME_CounterGet function, the following example
883	      will calculate the number of microseconds elapsed since timestamp was
884	      captured.
885	      <code>
886	      uint32_t count = SYS_TIME_CounterGet() - timestamp;
887	      uint32_t us    = SYS_TIME_CountToUS(count);
888	      </code>
889	
890	  Remarks:
891	     None.
892	*/

897	// *****************************************************************************
898	/* Function:
899	      uint32_t SYS_TIME_CountToMS ( uint32_t count )
900	
901	   Summary:
902	      Converts a counter value to time interval in milliseconds.
903	
904	   Description:
905	      This function converts a counter value to time interval in
906	      milliseconds, based on the hardware timer frequency as configured
907	      and as reported by SYS_TIME_FrequencyGet.
908	
909	   Precondition:
910	      The SYS_TIME_Initialize function should have been called before calling
911	      this function.
912	
913	   Parameters:
914	      count  - Counter value to be converted to an equivalent value in
915	               milliseconds.
916	
917	   Returns:
918	      Number of milliseconds represented by the given counter value.
919	
920	  Example:
921	      Given a previously captured uint32_t counter value called "timestamp"
922	      captured using the SYS_TIME_CounterGet function, the following example
923	      will calculate number of milliseconds elapsed since timestamp was
924	      captured.
925	      <code>
926	      uint32_t count = SYS_TIME_CounterGet() - timestamp;
927	      uint32_t ms    = SYS_TIME_CountToMS(count);
928	      </code>
929	
930	  Remarks:
931	      None.
932	*/
